Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair, I desire to bring to the attention of the House a matter that has been before the government for the last fifteen or sixteen years; that is, the question of the recognition in some substantial manner of the claims of the veterans of 1866 and 1870. I do not intend at this stage to go into the merits or demerits of the claims of the veterans, but I intend to show first of all what steps had been taken by the veterans with a view to having their rights recognized in some manner by this government, In the year 1896. I think, the first deputation waited on Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his government and asked for some Mr. FISHER,
recognition of their claims. In speaking to that deputation, the Prime Minister is reported as follows-I am reading now from ' Hansard ' of the 26th of March, 1906, and quoting from the speech made by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk):
He would like to find a few facts about the subject under discussion so that he would have a basis to work upon. To begin with, he said, I would like to know about how many men were called out at that time, and if it is the desire of the present delegation that services of all the remaining veterans who. took an laotive part and also in what way it is considered their services would best be recognized.
Further on the Prime Minister is reported as saying:
In making his reply, Mr. Laurier stated that he fully appreciated the strength of the reason that all should be remembered, and and that nothing would give him greater pleasure than laying the claims of the veterans before his colleagues at the next parliament, as he regretted to say it was too late at present to bring it up at the present session.
That would be towards the end of the first session of the present administration. Although between that time and 1905 two other delegations waited on the government, each of which received a favourable reply from the government, neither of which was specific, however, I un4erstand that in 1905 a further large delegation waited on the Prime Minister and Sir Frederick Borden, a delegation evidently composed largely of veterans from the eastern townships of the province of Quebec and some from the province of Ontario. To that delegation the Prime Minister is reported to have replied as follows:
Sir Wilfrid Laurier received much applause when "he rose to reply. Two years ago he had been approached by a smaller deputation on a similar errand, but as the session was far advanced he had been unable to give them a definite answer. He had told them then he hoped to be in a better position next time they came to him. The members had evidently remembered his words, for they had now returned in largely increased numbers. He could hardly claim to be a veteran, as they had called him, for he had only been a volunteer in 1870. When the regiment he belonged to had been mustered the trouble was over. To the victors, he said, belong the spoils, was an expression most of them were familiar with. While the veterans had turned back the invaders in 1866 and 1870 there had been no spoils left. Thirty years after they come to ask from the country some recognition for their services, and he thought some appreciation should be shown. Their services then bad (saved the country from much humiliation, if not worse. Had the invaders not been repelled at the border

much misery would have been caused, although, of course, the country would not have been conquered. What the veterans asked was not much. He could not give a definite answer himself to their request, but he could assure them that he and the ministers with him would be very pleased to report their request to the Privy Council. The meeting closed with three cheers and a 'tiger' for Sir Wilfrid, called for by some enthusiastic veteran.	[DOT]
In the same year the hon. member for Jacques Cartier again brought the matter up in the House, and at page 642 of Hansard of 1905, we find the Prime Minister reported as follows:
I think it is obvious to any one, and my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) will agree with me, that if the veterans of 1866 and 1870 have a claim against anybody, it is the Dominion government, although I do not say that the veterans, from their point of view, have not done well to address themselves to the provincial government. Mr. Gouin, the provincial premier, I do not think went further in his answer than to say that they should first of all address themselves to the Dominion government. This they have done, and the matter is now under consideration. But I must say, and my hon. friend will not be surprised, that up to this moment the government. has had no time to take the matter in 'hand and give it the attention which it will require before we can come to a conclusion.
I may just point out that although the government say they had not time to take the matter into consideration, it is exactly nine years since the veterans first presented their petition to the House. Then the Prime Minister went on to say:
The matter is under consideration, and without making any pledge, I will say that I will give an answer during the present session. When the answer will be given, I am sorry to say that I can give no indication today to my hon. friend, but certainly it will be given during the present session.
Well, the answer was not given during that session. A further deputation waited on the government in 1906 and laid their claims before it, and I find that on that occasion the following reply was mate to them by the Minister of Militia, Sir Frederick Borden:
But since my hon. friend has presented his argument and suggested that homesteads bona fide should be offered to these men who might be willing to go to the Northwest as actual settlers, I am inclined to the opinion that the government would be willing to take that matter into consideration.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE FENIAN RAIDS VETERANS.
speechtext: They have that privilege now.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE FENIAN RAIDS VETERANS.
speechtext:
That is what my hon. friend suggested, and I am merely giving him all he asks. I said a moment ogo that some advantages might be given in the way of offering them special privileges to settle in certain communities or in certain
favoured quarters. I have no right, however, to speak for the Minister of the Interior, but I would be disposed to go that far and see whether anything could he done to meet their views in that respect.
In the same debate the right hon. the Prime Minister is quoted as follows:
I dare say these veterans will say to us: We could fight in 1866, we could fight in 1870, but you canot expect that we can take up a pick and shovel and perform the arduous duties of a settler to-day. I can appreciate that answer, and I will say this, that if there is a man who cannot take his homestead we are ready to give it to him. If he has a son who is ready to fulfil the conditions of settlement, the government will be only too glad to give him that recognition. But if it is intended that these lands should be given to the veterans simply for the purpose of selling them to the foreigner, to the despised foreigner who has been mentioned by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier, that is a thing which 1 think would deserve a little consideration.
Further on the Prime Minister used these words:	[DOT]
This motion comes very late after a lapse of 40 years, but yet it is not too late, and if a plan can be devised by which we can leaven the mass with our own blood and find homesteads for our veterans or their descendants and children, the government would be pre-rpared to consider the question and do its share towards recognizing the men who risked their lives for the defence of the country upon that very important occasion.
I might here remark-that the Prime Minister said that this motion came very late. I would like to point out to him that in the year 1875 the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, then premier of the country, did not think that it was too late, after a period of 65 years, to grant an annual pension of $50,000 to the veterans who had served in the war of 1812. On page 252 of ' Hansard ' of 1875, I find the following:
On item 50-$50,000 to meet the probable amount required for pensions to veterans of the war of 1812*	*
Mr. KIRKPATRICK asked for some explanations. He desired to know whether those who had served for a shorter period, were to be placed on the same footing as those who had served for a long period, and whether all regiments would get a grant, or whether those known as the Glengarry regiment, which, he believed, had been pensioned by the Chelsea hospital authorities, were also to have a share. He also desired to know whether the widows of the veterans of 181-would receive any consideration.
Hon. Mr. CARTWRIGHT said he fesH?d they could, give nothing to the widows. I lie intention of the government was to give to all men in actual service, numbering, he believed, probably about five or six hundred - of course, they could not tell the exact number as some applications had come in which doubtless would not be fortified by the records. Those receiving aid must be at least

seventy-six or seventy-eight years of age, because the great number of those who took part in that war must now be about or over 80. The pensions would be as nearly as possible approaching the amount to those given to the pensioners of the regular army at home.
In reply to Mr. Flesher,
Hon. Mr. MACKENZIE said it was intended that the vote should be taken yearly. -Item passed.
So I would say that the mere fact that the volunteers o'f 1866 and 1870 have not been recognized after 40 years is no answer whatever, but on the contrary is only an argument why, if their claim is just, they should be recognized at this day, because the longer their rights are deferred the stronger their claims become. I would suggest that the Prime Minister follow the precedent of his former colleague and the former prime minister, Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, who thought it was not too late, after 65 years, to recompense those who had fought in the interests of their country.
Prom what I have read, I think it may safely be assumed that a promise was made in 1906 by the Prime Minister and by Sir Frederick Borden that something would be done, and I believe that many members on the Liberal side who at that time voted against the resolution of the hou. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), did so, believing that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Militia intended to give something substantial to the volunteers. In proof of that, I shall quote from a speech of Mr. Logan, of Hants, then a member of this House, who said:
I feel very much in sympathy with the idea of giving substantial recognition to the men who live and to the heirs of those who have died who fought at this time or who went to the front; and I might have been inclined to have voted in favour of the motion as put before the House if we had not had the .assurance given by the Minister of Militia and the Prime Minister, in reference to considering certain substantial recognition of what these men have done for their country.
So it is quite evident that in 1906, when this motion was before the House, many Liberals voted against it because they believed that the statements of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Militia amounted to a promise to do something
for these veterans, Mr. Logan said further on:
We believe the government will do its duty, with this promise which has been given by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Militia.

That was five years ago, yet nothing whatever lias been done to implement these promises.
I find that in the following years, with the perseverance and tenacity which they displayed in the rebellion, the veterans ccme back to the Prime Minister. In 1908, the Prime Minister replied to them as follows :
Two years ago I had the honour to receive a delegation of veterans of '66-'70 for the purpose of hearing a petition for recognition at the hands of the government. I did not then see a way of granting the petition. But I gave Mr. Patterson the injunction which I see he has remembered. Gentlemen, you have always been too kind to me. I cannot claim to be a veteran. True, I turned out with the rest, but I did so little that I am almost ashamed to wear my medal. But, gentlemen, there is an old saying that to the victors belong the spoils.
It is a peculiar thing that the Prime Minister has been holding up the spoils to these veterans the whole time, but they have not seen any of them yet. He continued :
After 30 years you come to your countrymen and ask that you may receive a little recognition at the hands of a grateful country- Something should be done. There is no doubt that by your action you saved the WttBtry from humiliation and perhaps worse. What you ask is not very much. But I am only one of the government. There are others here, the Postmaster General, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Militia, and we shall be pleased to present your request to the Privy Council and the Governor General. But, gentlemen, further than this I cannot promise.
The Prime Minister then added:
But do not trust the government.
That was in 1908. In the following teb-ruary they came and in the Toronto Globe,'
of February 5, I find this account of the meeting:
Sir Frederick Borden, after referring [to the medals granted, is reported as follows:

The ' Mail and Empire ' the same dale reports the meeting as follows:
Sir Wilfrid Laurier this afternoon promised [DOT]a deputation of men who took part in the Fenian Raids of 1866 and 1870 that he would recommend their request for a grant of land to His Excellency the Governor General at the earliest possible day.
That was in February, 1909, and still the veterans are kept waiting for the spoils which had been promised. Back again they come on December 3, a larger deputation than ever, and, on December 4, I find in the Toronto ' Globe ':
Veterans' requests-Sir Wilfrid's answer is very encouraging-Government already considering scheme of rewarding the men who repulsed the Fenian Raids.
One hundred and fifty Fenian Raid veterans of '66-'70 marched to Parliament Hill at noon to-day, headed by a pipe band, and met Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Sir Frederick Borden, Hon. Sydney Fisher and Hon. L. P. Brodeur. . . They asked either a land grant or pension. Sir Wilfrid Laurier in replying . . . said the government was always disposed to deal in a sympathetic spirit with the men who had stood ready to sacrifice their lives in defence of flag and country; but, while sympathizing with the movement for some tangible recognition of the veterans' claims, he thought there w'ould be some difficulty in deciding just who were entitled to the reward, and he intimated that perhaps it would be well to distinguish between the men who actually went to the front and saw active service and those who were merely under arms at the time of the raids. The matter was seriously engaging the attention of the government, and personally he would be glad if 6ome action could be taken soon to grant a reasonable measure of recognition to the veterans by a grateful country.

On the 30th of January, 1910, a question was put upon the Order Paper by the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) to which the government replied as follows: 303
The government has not come to any conclusion but will at an early day.
Just imagine, fourteen years after they came into power and after they had had it under their very serious consideration for fourteen years, they say that they still have it under their serious consideration. In the meantime there have been three general elections, in every one of which they received the support of the veterans on the assumption that they would get substantial recognition at the hands of the government.
In 1910, during his tour in the west, the Prime Minister is reported to have said:
We have had it under consideration some months and, without making any promises, I can say that something may be done.
Not very specific I admit, but a promise that something may be done. Then from August 10 there were continual interviews by Mr. Patterson with the government for the purpose of ascertaining what the government really intended, and I have here a letter addressed by Mr. Patterson who represents the association, to the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) dated April 20, 1910, which is as follows:
Sir Frederick Borden,
Minister of Militia,
Ottawa.
Honourable Sir,-Two weeks ago to-day, in the interview I had with you in your private office, yon stated you would bring the matter of federal grant to the veterans of '66 and '70 before the Privy Council on the following Saturday, lapsing our interview. You said you would push - the matter to a final decision, either a grant or the government would say no. You promised to communicate the results of your intention. Up to the present time I have not had the pleasure of hearing anything from you. Won't you kindly advise me by mail what has been done, or what is the intention, if any? Your reply will be appreciated by the veterans of the Dominion.
Yours faithfully,

In reply to this the Minister of Militia wrote as follows: And this, of course, was before the Prime Minister had taken his western trip in the course of which he said that something might be done:
Ottawa, May 9, 1910.
Dear Captain Patterson,-I must apologize for not having answered sooner your letter of the 28th August, but I am sure you will understand that I have been very busy ever since that date.
I have brought the matter of the veterans up in council on two occasions as promised, but unfortunately there was no time so late in the session to consider it. As I understood the feeling of the council, however, it was that there was a disposition to consider sympa-

thetically the claims of such of the veterans as actually went to the front and took part in repelling the would-be invaders, and with this object in view I feel sure that the Premier would be glad to receive you and any other colleagues whom the veterans might wish to associate with you and to discuss the manner in which this idea might be carried out.
I can only add that I shall be very glad at any time to join the Premier in assisting in such a discussion.
Yours very truly,

I think I am quite justified in saying, in view of the extracts that I have read from the remarks of the Prime Minister and his Minister of Militia, and from the correspondence, that the veterans were promised and had a right to expect some substantial consideration at the hands of this, government. I think I am justified in saying also that the debate of March 26, 1906, when the matter was brought up by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, showed that it was upon the express understanding that something was going to be done by tire government that many members on the Liberal side of the House voted against the resolution to give same substantial recognition to the veterans.
Apart altogether from the merits of the case, I think nobody will deny that the services to the country rendered by the veterans were rendered at the psychological moment in our history. One occasion was a year before Confederation. At that time there were large numbers of disbanded soldiers in the United States only too willing to fight. And had not our veterans come to the assistance of the country against these disbanded soldiers the destiny of Canada might have been entirely different from what it is. After confederation had been in existence only three years when the second occasion for the veterans to offer their assistance arose. At that time the United States had refused to continue the policy of reciprocity in natural products with this country; and those of the older generation know that at that time there was a very considerable feeling in this country that, because of the action of the United States, Canada would be compelled to throw in her lot with the United States. And, again, I say, the veterans came to the aid of the country at the psychological moment in that respect.
And it was owing at least in part to their action that the country was directed to a different destiny. These men lelt their businesses, their farms, their avocation at the call of duty. Permit me to read a portion of a letter from one of the veterans of that time which will illustrate better than any word I could speak the risks Mr. MIDDLEBRO.	/ [DOT]
these men ran, and the hardships they endured. This is a letter from one veteran to another:
Dear comrade,-It pleases me very much to learn that the veterans of the Fenian Raids of 1866 arid 1870 have formed a national association and are making a fight for recognition of the services which they (or rather we, for remember I am one of those veterans) have rendered our country almost half a century ago. Think of it, Charlie, it is just 45 years and 41 years ago respectively since the word of command ' to arms ' came from our beloved Colonel F. G. Marcliand, the late Prime Minister of the province of Quebec. The moment that command wa6 heard, men in shops dropped their tools, men in stores walked out from behind the counters, men in offices laid down tlieir pens, men on the farms left their ploughs where they stood, donned their uniforms, shouldered their rifles and in less than three hours the 21st .Battalion Richelieu Light Infantry was in line fully supplied with ammunition and ready to start for the front, which we did on the afternoon of the same day. The patriotism shown by the men of the 21st Battalion on that occasion was never equalled by the young men of any country, European or any other country, and the same spirit prevailed among the young men of the province. We cared not for our lives, we took that in one hand, our rifles iu the other and marched out to defend our country or die. ...	.
Many of us are to-day suffering from different ailments as a result of exposure and hardships experienced at that time. But, diu you ever hear any one complain? No, sir, I never have met one sad or dejected heart in all that campaign. Every man felt cheerful and was happy to be where he was and he knew he was doing his duty.
I believe that expresses the sentiment of the men who went to the front at that time. We have bad, since then, two precedents. The veterans of the rebellion of 1885 were given not only medals hut grants of land. The veterans of the South African war were given not only medals tout grants of land. If the grants made to these veterans are just and right, they create a precedent which cannot be ignored by this government. I can see no reason why the veterans of the present day should not be given some substantial recognition. It is not for me to say what form that recognition should take, whether a grant of land or a pension. If a pension, it is to he remembered that most of these men must be close to 80 years of age, and cannot live long. I think it is as little as the government can do to give some substantial recognition to these men who came to the aid of the country in time of stress. I move in amendment:
It is desirable that the government of Canada should recognize in some substantial manner the services rendered during the Fenian Raids of 1866 and 1870 by your Canadian volunteers.

But he has taken his course, and there is nothing to be done but to deal with his motion. The hon. gentleman stated that this question was fifteen or sixteen years old. He is altogether too modest-it is forty or forty-five years old.
My hon. friend invited me to act upon the precedent created by the government of Mr. Mackenzie in 1875, of which government I was a supporter. If there were any argument in that, perhaps my hon. friend would find a better and more adequate argument in the precedent created by the government of Sir John Macdonald who -was in office at the time these raids took place and which dealt with the case at that time. The government of Sir John Macdonald was in office in 1866, and, as he was the first Prime Minister of the Dominion his government was in office immediately after confederation, and until after 1870, the time the second raid took place. The veterans of that time did render valuable service to the country, undoubtedly. Those services were considered when they were fresh in the minds of the people of Canada and of the government of Canada. For reasons which I am not called upon to pass judgment upon, these claims were not entertained.
If the veterans of 1866 did that service for the country which my hon. friend says they did, and which they did emphatically, for some reason which I have not to appreciate-I did not belong to the party which was then in office, and my hon. friend does belong to that party-for some reason, at that time the government did not think it advisable to call upon the people of Canada to give them any recognition for the services they had performed. I
303$
think it is not to be expected that volunteers should give their services for a consideration, they do it simply out of patriotism; and if the government of that day took that position, what reason can be given to-day why we should reverse that judgment? There is, thei'efore, no argument in the fact that if the government in 1875 did recognize services which had been rendered to the country in 1812, we should do the same. We have adopted since then another method; we have now a more humane way of looking at those things. It is not a Conservative government which is in office, it is a Liberal government; but the Liberal government did recognize the services of the men who went to South Africa, and also, I think, the services of the men who went to the front in 1885 We gave them grants of land, and we did it out of the abundance of our heart; the Liberal party supported us in so doing. But I think my hon. friend must have heard echoes coming from the western portion of the community, especially that the policy adopted of giving grants of land to the ' eterans lui<l not turned out very much to the benefit of the country, or to the benefit of the veterans themselves. There are degrees of merit in the veterans. Some of them did very little service, if any at all. That was several years ago, but nothing has been done since. Some of the veterans have several times complained to me about the neglect with which they are treated, and I have never hesitated to state that so far as I was concerned, and the Conservative party as well, we would support any reasonable recognition of their services which

the government might propose. But to-day, we have this motion before us and there is not a single man on the Liberal side of the House to get up and say a word on behalf of these men who were out to fight, and to die if need be for their country.

I want to say a word in protest .of the position taken by the Prime Minister on this matter. I am satisfied that if he took a census of the people of the Niagara district, where the principal invasion referred to by my hon. friend took place, he would find that all those people, whether they were alive at that time or not, would be a unit in favour of this motion, because they know particularly well -what great services were rendered, in a very hurried and very philanthropic as well as patriotic and intelligent way, by those veterans. We in the Niagara district have never been able to understand why something in this respect was not done years ago. The Prime Minister has been quoted as having intimated from time to time that something of a substantial nature would be done. My hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) quoted the language of the Prime Minister, to which the Prime Minister replied, but he made no explanation or denial of the promises he had made. Therefore, I am justified in assuming as absolutely true that the Prime Minister did make the promises that were recited against him by the hon. member for North Grey. If he did, he stands obliged to support the motion. The right hon. gentleman's only reason for opposing the motion to-day is that he does not think it opportune, and -does not approve of the manner in which it is brought up. For the life of me I cannot understand what the Prime
Minister does want done. He makes promises in regard to this matter, and he does not fulfil them; his ministers make promises, and he does not say they should fulfil them, and when a humble member of the opposition undertakes to help him to fulfil them, he wants none of them. He does not want his promises carried out by any one if he does not propose to carry them out himself. If he wanted some excuse for doing this long-delayed justice to these people, he has every excuse in the declarations which have been made by the opposition in this House over and ovpr again for a number of years past, that they were willing to vote for any measuie which would extend some substantial recognition to the class of patriots referred to in this motion. The application of these people no one has dared to reject on the merits. It is not only the veterans who are concerned; the nationality of Canada, the integrity of this -portion of the British Empire and the integrity of the empire as a whole is concerned. If invasion were threatened tomorrow, ten times the number who enlisted on that occasion would be prepared to enlist to protect this country from any invader, but foreign countries will have very little respect for the Dominion if it f&jis to recognize in some substantial way the patriotism shown by these veterans on the occasions to which this motion refers. The example to the rest of the world is a bad one. This country practically insults itself when it refuses- a motion such as that made to-day, after all these years. The government that undertakes to reject such a motion and offers nothing in its place, practically tells the world that it does not care anything about gratitude towards the people who may protect the country. Those of us who were not on hand at that time are just as much interested from a national point of view as the descendants of those who were. We were served by those people, our nationality, and our' integrity as a part of the British Empire were protected by them, and this -country owes it to itself to do justice to the veterans who served it on those occasions. The Prime Minister has not told us why this motion is inopportune. Is it inopportune simply because the Prime Minister has neglected his duty for the last 10 years? But here is the point: These men have b'en led to believe all these years after having established their claim, that their services would be given some recognition. They have established their claim morally and one might almost say legally. They mve not established it on the ground of technical legality, that is of making it enforcible in the courts, but they have established it leg-

speechtext:
The remarks of my hon. friend from Sliefford (Mr. Allen) clearly demonstrates to my mind the insincerity of the government in dealing with this question, and the pitiable level to which, by the action of the Prime Minister, this great national question, involving the national honour of Canada, has been dragged down to the lowest level of party politics.	_
What is the position, as illustrated in the very exhaustive speech of the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) in support of this motion? I believe that, as my hon. friend from Shefford (Mr. Allen) is convinced that this is a righteous claim and that these veterans are justly entitled to this recognition, the majority of this House are in favour of the principle of this resolution, and that were it not for the lash applied to them by the Prime Minister in his speech this afternoon there would be a majority in favour of the resolution of the hon. member for North Grey. What a lamentable spectacle has been presented upon a question of national importance in which national honour is involved? Here are a set of men-I do not want to recapitulate the value of the services that they rendered to this country1-who left their homes, and their business, who made great sacrifices of their interests, and at great danger to themselves and privation to their
families, rushed to the border to defend their country against invaders, the country of which we are now so proud, which hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House are never tired of extolling. They ask :in a very moderate way for such recognition as has been given in other instances to other Canadians who have fought in Canada's interests as well as in the interest of the empire. What is the answer that is made to these men? For fifteen years, during the term of the administration of this government, they are put off with different excuses and promises, all of which involve sympathetic consideration of their case. The hon. member for Shefford prefers to believe that this government will give some relief to these veterans although it is upon the records of this House, out of the mouth of the responsible minister the Minister of Militia and Defence-that the government has no such intention at ail, and that in so far as the government is concerned the matter is closed. _ What a sublime faith this one of the Tight hon. gentleman's followers has in his government notwithstanding the fact that they have placed themselves on record as being unwilling to do anything. What position does the hon. member for Shefford find himself in to-day? He is in sympathy with the motion; will he vote for it? No, he will vote for the right hon. leader of the government and why? Because he is subject to the whin. My hon. friend believes and has sought to express the belief that this government will, and should do something for these veterans, and, notwithstanding the fact that the Minister of Militia has said in answer to a definite question that nothin1* will be done, he will vote to reject this motion. It is a lamentable spectacle in connection with a great national question, and a question involving national honour and duty. Not to grant this recognition would be to leave a blot upon the fair escutcheon of Canada, and it is lamentable, I repeat, that a question of this kind cannot be dealt with in this House without the whip of the party being brought into play in order to make the followers of the government vote, as I believe they will vote, contrary to their sympathies in this case.
But, there is another view of this question which strikes me as being somewhat peculiar. We have large tracts of land out in the Northwest; we have thrown these open to settlement upon liberal terms free to who ever will till the ground and otherwise comply with the homestead regulations. The lands of the Northwest have been Used for other purposes, for rewards for those who have served the country and the empire, a fact which has been referred to by my hon. friend from North Grey, and other hon. gentlemen who have followed him. The right hon. leader of the govern-

ment has taken a strangely inconsistent position upon this question. He admits that the men who went to the Northwest in 1885 to quell the rebellion were properly rewarded by grants of land belonging to the government, and he further consents to the giving out large parcels of thfike lands to those of our Canadian boys who answered the call of empire and fought in South Africa in 1889, 1890 and the following year. Where is the consistency of the Prime Minister now in refusing to accept the resolution introduced by my hon. friend from North Grey? The right hon. gentleman does not like to see Canada mixed up in the empire's wars. In London, not long ago, he distinguished himself, (or extinguished himself) in the view of the Candian people, by laying down the proposition, shocking to the consciences and feelings of a number of the empire's citizens, that Canada should not be drawn into the empire's wars without her consent. Yet, Sir, when our boys, responding to the call of the empire, went to South Africa, reluctant as the Prime Minister was on that occasion to give his consent for them to go, and when they came back he rewarded them with federal land grants in the west. What a strange inconsistency is manifested now by the right hon. gentleman? When Canada was in the dawn of its present development, when it was in the twilight of the magnificent prosperity which now blesses it, and which we hope shall hereafter bless it, these men responded to the call of their country for the protection of their homes, our homes, our land, our heritage and rushed to the border willing to lay down their lives if necessary as good Canadians in the cause of Canada, and yet the right hon. leader of the government, out of the great loyalty of his heart, posing as a great Canadian, says that there shall be no reward for these men, no land grant of any kind whatsoever, and calls upon this House to vote down the resolution of my hon. friend from North Grey. That is a strange spectacle for the right hon. gentleman to present to the Canadian people at this time, and in conjunction with the course which he has taken in regard to Canada's position in imperial wars.
It is well to notice what the reasons are that guide the Prime Minister in taking this somewhat questionable stand. Has he given any reason why these men should not be rewarded suitably? No, Sir, he has not, but he has broken straws with reference to the case of the veterans by alluding to the inactivity of the previous government in dealing with the question. What has that to do with the case? For fifteen years the right horn gentleman has jockeyed with the situation, has jollied these veterans, and has given them expressly to believe Mr. BOYCE.
that they would be rewarded in a substantial manner by this government.
Why, at the last moment, should he endeavour by flimsy excuse to avoid the real issue and attempt to throw the responsibility upon his predecessors in office. The question before this House is whether these veterans are going to get long delayed justice; whether the government will recognize the moral claim of these men to recognition, as they have promised. I am strongly in accord with the resolution now before the House, and I think the nonadoption of it would leave a blot upon the fair name of Canada and leave outstanding a national debt of honour which Canada ought to pay. Large grants of land have been made to friends of the government for political purposes; men who have-sat in this House have been enriched tremendously by grants of land from the government obtained through means open to criticism and suspicion. Foreign immigrants are encouraged to come here by offering blocks of free land; steamship and immigration agents have been paid by this government so much per head to induce foreign immigrants to take up the land and till it, but have not the veterans-a greater claim to their own soil? Are not those who have fought for Canada in her dire need entitled to recognition before foreigners who have Ijo be bonused to come here? I earnestly hope that the resolution of my hon. friend (Mr. Middlebro) will receive greater consideration than has been shown it by the Prime Minister. I hope hon. gentlemen opposite will vote iu accordance with their principles and that my hon friend from Shefford (Mr. Allen) will vote in accordance with bis expressed conviction, and by so doing free Canada from a blot on her escutcheon.

We have in these words the distinct understanding that at least one supporter of the government believed that the P rime Minister, and the Minister of Militia would provide some tangible recognition of the claims of the veterans. But, the attitude of the government on this question since 1906 has been uncertain, indefinite, and equivocating; they have led the veterans along, pursuing a will-o'-the-wisp, without ever implementing their promises. To-day the Prime Minister wants to know why the government of Sir John A. Macdonald did not do something, but I tell him that the government of Sir John A. Macdonald looked after the widows and orphans of those killed and pensioned those wounded, and did everything then asked of them. Deputation	after deputation has waited on the Prime Minister, and the Minister of Militia without ever obtaining a definite promise, but to-day the government will be forced to say yes or no to this resolution. I regret the language of the Prime Minister in which he apparently belittled the great services these veterans have rendered to the country. He said that he himself had secured a medal, and did not deserve it, but it does seem extraordin-try that he should make application for a medal if he felt that his services did not entitled him to get one. The men of 1866 and 1870 responded to the call of their country; they endured the hardships of a daily drill from the month of March till the month of June; they came under fire; they made greater sacrifices than some of the volunteers who went to South Africa, and who never set foot on the shores of that country, but whose services were nevertheless recognized by a land grant. The quick response of the men of 1866 and 1870 to the call of their country and their determined resistance to the invading enemy possibly changed the destiny of this country, so that their great services are not to be slighted. I call attention to the treatment accorded to the veterans of 1866 and 1870 by the Ontario government. It would seem to me that the attitude of the federal government is brought about in a measure by the fact that the majority of these veterans lived in the province of Ontario, and this seems another instance of unjust discrimination by the present Dominion government against that province. We have standing between us and the proposal for a commercial invasion of this country, a proposition to reward those who were instrumental in resisting an armed invasion at the time of confederation. We are brought here in the dog days, in the close season for legislation, because of the statement of the government that a promise by a minister of the Crown, an unauthorized promise even, is so sacred that we must go to this extreme means to implement it. We are confronted by this other promise of the First Minister and other ministers that they would do something substantial for the veterans of 1866, and when this proposition is before the House we are told in effect that the word of a minister of the Crown in Canada is of variable value, that it is something substantial when given to ministers of another country seeking to take advantage of Canadian simplicity to prey upon the resources of this country, but that the

word of a minister of the Crown, of the First Minister, is of no value at all wheu given simply to a private soldier of the King who has gone out to active service in defence of his country.
Mr. Speaker, I do not believe that the people of this country will relish the assumption that they are willing to subscribe to the monstrous doctrine that the word of a minister given to an elector of Canada in the hope that it may induce that elector to support this ministry is not of equal value with the word of a minister given to any foreign country. There is a widely-voiced opinion in this country, that this parliament, so far as its governing majority is concerned, is dead, and that we have come to the House at this inopportune season simply to set a date for the obsequies. If anything were needed to justify that popular impression, in which I concur, it is the spectacle presented in this House this afternoon of the majority supporting the government having absolutely nothing to say in defence of the extraordinary position taken by the Prime Minister, their answers to the arguments on this side being simply that which we have had presented to us so often during the last few years-' We have more heads than you have, count them.' And the fact that the silence of these gentlemen has not been prompted by their conviction that everything has been said that should be said in defence of the position that they propose to vote for is well illustrated by the unfortunate break made by the only follower of the right hon. the Prime Minister having the temerity to address the House on this occasion. The right hon. the Prime Minister, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, told us that this matter was settled, that it had been settled by the answers that the Minister of Militia placed upon the records of this House. But why, if we desire to reward these veterans, should we confine ourselves to grants of land in view of our experience with similar grants that we have made. It is well known to the government, and to every member of this House that when you give as a reward to a veteran or any other person a grant of land, the country pays the full value of that land whether the individual to whom it is offered gets the value, or whether he is forced to divide it with some intermediary who may be in a position to deal with, if not settle upon the land. Now, since the country has to pay the full value, why not ensure that the proposed recipient of the grant should have the whole value and not have to share it with the middlemen who have done so much harm in operations of this kind? The Prime Minister, knowing the experience we have had, knowing that it will cost no more to hand out the absolute value to the veterans than to give them grants of land to be preyed upon by speculators, has before him the immediate solution of one of the difficulties that presents itself to his mind. It is only necessary for him to give to the veterans the value, instead of grants of land such as have been shown to be so unprofitable if not unpopular. The right hon. gentleman told us also that we were confronted with a serious difficulty because it would be absurd to offer grants of land to every person who was mustered in connection with the repelling of the Fenian raid. He said there would have to be discrimination. And what we were told by the right hon. gentleman would lead one to believe that in none of the other grants of this kind had we exercised this discrimination. But the record is to the contrary. When we rewarded the veterans of the Northwest campaign of 1885, we did not hand out grants of land and medals to all those who mustered on that occasion. We drew the line at a certain degree of service which should entitle the men to the grant of land. We gave the benefit of the doubt to the volunteer in every case, so that it could not be said that any fine drawn distinctions were made to deprive any man of his reward. Speaking from memory I think the line of distinction in that -case was that all the troops mustered for the occasion who proceeded west of the Lakes were given the reward of a grant of land, while those who were mustered, but remained at home were not given the grant. speechtext: I am sure the members of the government as well as all the members of the House have learned with the greatest anxiety of the condition of affairs, at Porcupine, and have the very warmest sympathy with those who have suffered so much in that disaster. We have had representations made to us through a committee of gentlemen in Ottawa particularly but they were not able to give us a very extended report as to the nature of the disaster and the need for assistance. Indeed, it has been represented by gentlemen to whose views we are bound to give consideration, that while the disaster is one of very considerable extent, and attended by many distressing circumstances, there is no immediate need of aid; that is to say, that the aid that has already been given is sufficient for all purposes, and that several weeks perhaps might elapse before we could be fully advised as to the extent of the misfortune and the need of assistance. It is even stated by a prominent gentleman interested in that part of Ontario that every need of the community is now being attended to. However, we quite realize that the information in the possession of the government, as it is in the possession of the public generally, is of a general and somewhat indefinite character, and we think it would be well that we should await some further information before coming to a decision as to what action may be necessary, if necessary, to provide the desired relief. Relief, perhaps in the most useful and substantial form, was sent immediately, in the form of canvas tents, which are being used to cover the people. That I understand has been very useful. Indeed, in itself it involves a very substantial aid. But whether or not the need will arise for further aid is a point on which the government are awaiting further information.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I see the hon. Postmaster General in his place, I desire to bring to the attention of the House and the country an improvement that could be made by the action of the government in the telegraph and cable services of this country. We have heard a good deal in Canada for some years about public ownership. I believe it is a great principle; I believe it has

great promise and great performance for the public of Canada. We have talked about it for quite a while, and we have realized it in a way.. In the province of Ontario we have realized that principle in a way that justifies it. Public ownership is based on the idea that it will first of all give the public a greatly improved service, and, in the next place, that it will give the public a much cheaper service. Now, that has been denied; but we have to-day the evidence of all Europe, of Australia, of New Zealand, of other countries, that the principle of public ownership is a great success. In Ontario we have tried it, and the very first result of the operation of the HydroElectric Commission in that province has been to cut the price of a widespread public service in two, and to improve the service. In the city of Toronto, where an electric monopoly held up the citizens and gave a very poor service we have to-day the price cut in two, and a service owned and controlled by the people of Toronto, which promises to be an excellent service. In this House itself, where the lighting is by electricity, we make a contract with a private company for a certain candle-power. Do you ever get it? No. There is such an absence of juice, to use a technical term, in the service, that sometimes the lights are not equal to eight candle-power where we have been promised 32. In the city of Hamilton, where there was a monopoly controlled by the Cataract Power Company, the moment there is public ownership, what does the private monopoly say? It says, we will give you as good or a better price than the Hydro-Electric. And so the principle of public ownership has vindicated itself in the province of Ontario in connection with a great system of lighting for all the municipalities of that province. The province of Ontario, whether it is patriotic or not, is to-day selling or is about to sell power to the citizens of the United States for less than they can buy it for elsewhere.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE FENIAN RAIDS VETERANS.
speechtext: That is reciprocity.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE FENIAN RAIDS VETERANS.
speechtext:
Yes, but it is a different kind of reciprocity from that which the government is proposing. We have tried public ownership in the Dominion in connection with the Intercolonial railway, but that public ownership was never given an opportunity to make good. Put the Intercolonial railway in competition with other railways; extend it to Toronto, to the Georgian bay, to the Detroit river, and railway rates in the province of Ontario would be cut one-third in a single day, and the government railway would be a success. The Intercolonial railway should have been put into the great Canadian west, and then there would have been a reduction in rates that would have substantially benefited the 304J
people of the west. You cannot vindicate government ownership of railways unless you give the principle a fair chance to vindicate itself. And to-day, even though the Canadian Pacific railway is bound by its contracts to give the people of the west lower freight rates, we are told we must not enforce the law against the Canadian Pacific railway because it would injure the Grand Trunk Pacific and Canadian Northern railway. Now, as to the post office, the telegraph, and the cable services. True, we have tried government owned telegraphs in this country, but only in uninhabited parts on the Atlantic coast, on the Pacific coast, and up to the Yukon where public owner-shin had no opportunity to serve the people. The time has come when the post Office Department must take over the telegraphs, or else they must extend the existing government owned wires into a transcontinental service so as to compete with the railway monopoly of telegraphs. The telegraph tolls to-day in the Canadian west are exorbitantly high, and the telegraph company that controls the service in the west is reaping enormous profits. The profits of the Canadian Pacific Railway Telegraph service in the west ought to be reduced at once, and if we cannot reduce them by form of law we should immediately resort to the establishment of a government owned transcontinental telegraph service. The day has arrived when there ought to be a national transcontinental telegraph service throughout Canada and connecting with all the great cities of the country. Then, in conjunction with that, cable tolls should be reduced, and the effective way to reduce cable tolls is for Canada to establish an Atlantic cable. The business now offering is more than the existing Atlantic cable companies can do; there is room for competition, and I believe that the mere announcement that the government of Canada would adopt the principle of government ownership in cables would result in a reduction from the present commercial rate of 25 cents a word to 5 cents a word, and the business community of the world would be enormously benefited. You may talk of the Steel Trust and other great monopolies, but there is no such powerful monopoly in the world to-day as the Eastern Telegraph Company in England. They largely control the cables all over the world; they are probably the most influential corporation in England, and they have had more influence at government head quarters in England for the last 50 years, and especially with the late government, than any other corporation. Do what you might it has been impossible to get the Eastern Telegraph Company to reduce its exorbitant rates or to improve its service. I believe the Postmaster General (Mr. Le-mieux) has taken part in negotiations held

in England, and that a promise has been made that cable rates would be reduced, but so far the public has derived no benefit in that direction. Perhaps it may come from the present discussion in this House, but anyway, come it should. The principle of government ownership so well vindicated in Onti rio in connection with the distribution of c- fectric power can easily and cheaply be appl id to telegraphs and cables, for it will not !ost much to build one or two cables aero i the Atlantic to start with, and then will fc low a cable to Australasia if that be necessi ,y to control the service on the Pacific. II has been mentioned in the press, and in parliament that a reduction in cable tolls is in sight, but it will not be realized by talking about it; government ownership of the telegraphs and cables is the real cure for the existing evil. Great Britain has adopted the principle in connection with her inland telegraph system, she is adopting it with reference to her telephone system, and Germany, and Russia, and Japan, and China, and Australia, and New Zealand, where their system has been tried would not give up their control for any consideration. Then, government ownership of telegraphs and cables would not only cheapen the rates, but it would widen the area of the effectiveness of the service.
Where there were 3,000 or 4,000 telegraph offices in the mother country they now have 12,000 or 15,000. The improved system has been a great success. We in Canada are to-day paying exorbitant telegraph and cable tolls. We can have them reduced by the application of the principle of public ownership. We can easily get the money to establish the new system and we can insist on the mother country joining with us in the project because Great Britain is now committed to the principle and there is a great imperial reason, there is a great reason of peace behind the proposition which I urge here to-day. We are today discussing arbitration treaties in the world. Great Britain and the United States are binding themselves one to the other in favour of a system of arbitration in place of a resort to war. That idea, which we all welcome, is making great headway but if the principle of arbitration is to govern, it can only realize itself by having the support of a world wide public opinion and a world wide public opinion can only be created by the rapid interchange of public opinion between different countries by means of a cheap cable telegraph service. It is in the interest of this country, in the interest of peace, in the interest of business, in the interest of the empire that there should be cheaper telegraph and cable tolls and we can never get them to the full until the state undertakes to build telegraph lines and to be a party, along with other states of the empire, in the construction and main-Mr. MACLEAN.
tenance of the state-owned cables, if that is the case why is not the principle recognized? It will do everything for the country. It will be a boon to the farmer of the west. Those farmers are told that they want the American market. Perhaps they do. Perhaps the Americans will give it to them off their own bat. By all means let them do so if they wish to, but let tne farmers get relief from the exorbitant telegraph tolls now exacted from them. The railway commission have not yet caught up with all their work, they have not yet reduced the telegraph tolls to any great extent. But those tolls would be reduced at once by the mere threat to start a state owned telegraph system. We have had the fruit now in Ontario; the city of Toronto is about to realize it in connection with its street railway. They proposed to establish a municipal system as they have a right to do in competition with the private owned principle and the moment that was done there was an improvement in the ser -vice, a cheapening in the price and an enlargement in the area of the application of the service. My contention is that the government or the Postmaster General representing the government should tell the people of Canada what all these negotiations up to the present have resulted in and whether we are to have cheaper cable telegraph tolls or whether the government are prepared, if they cannot get it by negotiation, then to. come forward and give tlie people and press of Canada the benefit of a state-owned system. They have given some relief to the press in connection with cable tolls because those tolls were so exorbitant that the newspapers were not able even to transmit the ordinary news of the day between Canada and the mother country. The government is committed to that principle to-day in relation to the press but they have not realized it for the public; the press get a ten cent rate and the government help to pay the difference, but if the government will-establish state owned cables and land lines jointly with the Imperial government, first connecting the great cities of Canada like Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto, Winnipeg, Calgary and Vancouver, the interest on the investment would be easily paid and the telegraph rates would be cut in three. There is a substantial opportunity to benefit the people of all this country by giving them a state owned telegraph and cable service.
It is true the Prime Minister said he is afraid of public ownership. I do not know whether the Postmaster General (Mr. Le-mieux) is also afraid but if he has been afraid in the past he has that living example in Ontario that the moment they embarked in earnest on the project of public ownership applied to the distribution of electricity, one of the greatest blessings in

the world, to the people, the price was cut in two, the service was improved, and distribution was made all over the province. The work has only begun but at the very first inception of it the coon comes down. The late Attorney General of Ontario-1 shall not speak of him by his present title-devoted himself to creating a great monopoly in Ontario in connection with the electric service, especially in connection with the city of Hamilton. It never would amount to anything and the special pleaders now in Hamilton and all over Ontario are say;ng it will not amount to anything, it will not realize itself; but it has realized itself to-day and we in Toronto have had our electric prices cut in two. We have done more than that, we have disciplined the competing companies. They are civil now to the public, they take off their hats and ask what they can do for their customers. They have to do for every city what they do for any one city and if, by competition of the government they are forced to give consideration and to give concessions in one place they must by parity of reasoning give them to other places. So the result of public ownership, this much derided principle, in Ontario to-day is that it has realized itself and yet, it has only started. It is the greatest project that any state has undertaken and is almost the widest exposition of the principle we have seen for a long while. But it has been successful from the start and it comes home to us in this House in connection with the government of Canada to see if we cannot apply that principle of government ownership to the telegraph and cable services of this country and of the empire in such a way as to bring about an improvement and cheapening of these services.
So I would like to -hear some account of these negotiations, a statement of what the result has been or if no result is in sight when the government would be prepared to take up the question of improving the cable service of the country and the land telegraph lines in such a way as to afford substantial benefit to the country, we can do a great deal. We can bring relief to-morrow to the farmers of the west in connection with telegraph tolls and to all Canada in connection with Tailway rates, a still greater question, if we have the courage and the capacity to apply the principle of public ownership to the railway problem of this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would have preferred to have had my hon. friend give me notice of his intention to bring this matter up this evening. However, I will state in a few words how tne question stands in regard to cable rates. First, let me tell him, speaking personally and for myself alone, that I am not so much averse
in many respects to public ownership. As my hon. friend stated, in the older countries such as France, England and Germany and in newer countries from the point of view of civilization, such as Japan, the Post Office Department includes all communications and in those countries telephones, telegraphs and cables are under post office jurisdiction.
In this country, however, we have not yet reached that stage, although there is a strong movement, in some parts of the country in favour of public ownership of this form of public utility. We have, however, made a very important step in that direction by the establishment of the Railway Commission. My hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean) knows that any person can bring before the Railway Commission the telegraph companies or telephone companies, or even the cable companies, if it is believed that their rates are excessive.
My hon. friend stated that there had been some discussion between the Post Office Department in Great Britain and the Canadian Post Office. That is quite true. On two different occasions, it was my duty to discuss with the Postmaster General in England the question of cable rates. There was a strong opinion in this country that the rates should be cut. I found also two friends of cheaper rates in the two Postmasters General with whom I have discussed this matter, Mr. Buxton and Mr. Samuels. Mr. Buxton, who is now president of the Board of Trade, was strongly in favour of cheaper cable communication between Canada and the mother country. Like his predecessor, Mr. Samuels, with whom I had some interviews last year, he agreed that in some way or other means should be found to reduce the rates. We even discussed what schedule of rates should be established. I may say that we reached the following basis in case we were able to bring the cable companies to terms : The actual rate of 25 cents per word was to be maintained for what we called ' urgent cables '. Twelve cents a word was to be charged for the semi-urgent messages. My contention was that we should have another reduction for the press to a rate of six cents a word. Without at all committing my colleagues on the other side of the water, Messrs. Buxton and Samuels, I may say we were practically agreed upon these rates. But in England the cable companies have thousands of shareholders and it was thought that perhaps it would injure vested rights if the government should press too hard on the cable companies in order to bring them to terms. I am passing very rapidly over the various discussions we had; but. later in the session, if my hon. friend will renew his motion, I may bring before the House the papers I have in the denartment relating to the subject, and from these he will gain more information

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE FENIAN RAIDS VETERANS.

speechtext:
than I can give him this evening. Last year it was finally agreed that the cable companies should reduce their rates by 12i cents on the semi-urgent messages, provided these messages were not in cipher, and provided also that a certain time should be allowed for delivery.-I think it was 20 or 24 hours. Before recess, I received a letter from Mr. Samuels stating that there remained one country, France, to join in the general agreement made by the various European cable companies. The government of Germany and of Great Britain had agreed. I have not received any further information from Mr. Samuels since that time, but I dare say that in a very short time announcement can be made that a reduction is made from 25 cents a word on ordinary cable messages to 12 cents a word. But I wish to go further than that. My hon. friend is aware that the question was brought up at the last Imperial Conference. Again I say that I am speaking on my own responsibility. I am personally in favour of a state-owned cable between Canada and Great Britain. I am not what some people call a jingo; I am a sane imperialist and I think that if you wish to forge the bonds of union among the different parts of the empire, you must have cheap electric communication so as to make the centre of the empire the nerve centre of the imperial organization. There are objections to that, of course, and I agree that we cannot overcome such objections by a wave of the hand. As my hon. friend is aware, a motion was made in the last Imperial Conference in favour of a state-owned cable. The reduction of which 1 have spoken was referred to by the British Postmaster General, Mr. Samuels, wh'o said that the reduction would be made within a short time. But he committed himself and the British government to a further reduction to be obtained from the cable companies, otherwise a state-owned could would have to be established. I think that is the gist of the resolution adopted by the conference. So, if my hon. friend and the press, who arc very much interested in these matters, and the public generally, will be patient, I think the day ' is not far distant when we shall have cheaper communication by elecricity between Canada and the motherland. I am sure my hon. friend is aware that the question of the land lines is not a great difficulty after all. We have to-day a land line leased for the Pacific cable between Vancouver and Montreal. There is a very little gap between Montreal and Quebec, and from Quebec and the maritime provinces we could use the government telegraphs. It would be a very small matter to provide a cable between the two coun-tne*. According to figures which have been verified by experts it would cost something like $2,000,000 or a little more to establish Mr. LEMIETJX.
cable communication between Canada and Great Britain. Another objection which prevents the home government from committing themselves absolutely to state-owned cables at present is the outlook for Mr. Marconi's invention. Mr. Marconi has been very successful, and it is believed in England that he will go much farther and that perhaps, when he has mastered his invention it will be a much less expensive matter to establish a system of communication between England and Canada than by means of a cable.
I may say to my hon. friend that last year the Imperial government purchased all the rights of the Marconi system in Great Britain; to-day the Marconi stations in England, Ireland and Scotland are the property of the state; and it is intended, when Mr. Marconi has perfected his system, to take full control of the invention. At a later stage of the session, I hope to be able to give the House more information on this question.

The delegates of the various colonies and the Postmaster General in England himself are not satisfied with this reduction, they want a further reduction; if they do not get it they have committed themselves to the establishment of a state-owned cable.

speechtext: The moment the reduction is accepted, the moment there is no burden on the public, there will be no necessity of state ownership.

speechtext:
I do not know if I am in a position to answer my hon. friend's question without having the papers before me. The government in England and the cable companies agreed that the present rate of 25 cents should remain as it is for urgent messages. My hon. friend knows that during certain hours of the day the cables are busy with messages from the various bourses of the world, and those people do not care whether a message costs 25 cents or even $1 a word. But for the general publie, for social messages and
even business messages, provided they are not in code or cipher, and provided there is no obligation about their delivery within a specified time, say within 24 hours, the cable companies have agreed to reduce the rate to 12 cents a word. But that is not thought sufficient by the parties who have made the agreement, and at the last Imperial conference the question came up, and it was decided that the British Postmaster General should urge upon the cable companies a still further reduction in their rates, and if they do not yield to the pressure of the government, there is an implied promise that there will be a state owned cable.
Motion agreed to, and House went into committee on Ways and Means.

The Prime Minister laughs, and provided he can persuade his people to give him another term in office it is a matter of indifference to him how many years of repentance will follow their sad experience.
In 1867 confederation came, and with dt the hope which had previously been confined to a few ardent patriots-that Canada would become a nation within a nation, and would work out her destiny as such-spread to the mass of our people; and there and then began one of the most courageous and difficult and patriotic enterprises which has ever been witnessed, viz.: the building up upon half a continent, by a handful of people, of a great Dominion, and the overcoming of enormous natural difficulties and disadvantages.
Consider, for a moment, the difficulties to be overcome. The British North America Act, Canada's constitution, first united Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and provided for the union of Prince Edward Island and British Columbia and the vast territories between British Columbia and Hudson bay and extending from the United States boundary to the Arctic ocean. Canada's task was to weld all these into one Dominion and to provide for its government, and to preserve its autonomy and British connection.

British Columbia came in on the 20th of July, 1871, and Prince Edward Island on the 1st of July, 1873. This first part was comparatively easy.
