If the farmer believes he is going to be benefited by the small reductions which are being made in manufactured articles according to this list, he is absolutely being misled. But this idea is being sedulously spread throughout all Canada to-day. We find large quantities of literature going out from the government side teaching this idea, but we do not find them sending out any literature giving the actual facts. Now,
I intend to oppose this reciprocity agreement for three principal reasons. In the first place, I believe it is unwise for ns Canadians to entangle ourselves at the present time, commercially or otherwise, with the United States. That country has always been our most formidable competitor commercially. I believe the United States has entered into this bargain with the idea that they are getting the best of it, and that in the end it will lead to the annexation of Canada by the United States. In the second place, I believe that no fiscal change as great as this should be entered into by Canada, making such radical change in our tariff conditions, without the people of Canada being consulted. In the third place, I believe the treaty in itself would lie of no benefit to Canada, but would be most injurious to the farmers of this country. and would put many of our Canadian
industries under the control of the trusts of the United States, of which we already have enough of our own. Now I do not mean to say, and I do not think, that hon. gentlemen sitting on the other side of the House are less loyal than those sitting on this side of the House, but I believe they are mistaken. I believe they entered into this agreement without understanding its full import, and I believe that those of them who have studied the question carefully, if it were not for their party loyalty would be absolutely opposed to this agreement at the present time. Now there is no question as to what the Americans think of it. They have shown no hesitation in expressing their opinions, and at the risk of weaTying the House, I would like to quote a few extracts from leading American statesmen showing what they think will be the effect of this agreement. First, I will quote a statement from President Taft: One path leads to practical if not political union with Canada, and the development of the entire North American continent as the heritage and the possession of a great and free people. The other path leads to the hardening into two distinct political entities, two hostile or at least unsympathetic peoples on this continent. It leads to a closer relation between Canada and Great Britain. It means the carrying out of Joseph Chamberlain s

great dream of a British imperial federation, bound together no less by trade than by sentiment, with preferential tariffs on either side, with Canada taking the place of the United States as chief purveyor of food products and manufactures to Great Britain.
To-day England is our best customer, and Canada is our third best customer. But our foreign trade wanes, and that of Canada grows. If we push Canada into England's arms, the trade larrangements between the two will tend more and more to shut us out.
How long will our trade with these two customers last, if reciprocity fails? Our Canadian must drop off, as the east and west channels of her commerce are scoured by us. And Canada will more and more supply English needs in our stead.
Again, speaking on page 8 of the American ' Congressional Record,' we find Mr. Taft saying:
The benefit to our widespread agricultural implement industry from the reduction of Canadian duties in the agreement is clear Similarly the new, widely distributed and expanding motor vehicle industry of the United States is given access to the Dominion market on advantageous terms. . . That the broadening of the sources of food supplies, that the opening of the timber resources of the Dominion to our needs, that the addition to the supply of raw materials, will be limited to no particular section does not require demonstration. The same observation applies to the markets which the Dominion offers us in exchange. As an illustration, it has been found possible to obtain free entry into Canada for fresh fruits and vegetables-a matter of special value to the south and to the Pacific coast in disposing of their products in their season. . . The entire foreign trade of Canada in the last fiscal year, 1910, was $655,000,000. The imports were $376,000,000, and of this amount tire United States contributed more than $223,000,000. The reduction in the duties imposed by Canada will largely increase this amount and give us even a larger share of her market than we now enjoy, great as that is.
Mr. Beveridge, speaking at Washington said:
There must be reciprocity with Canada. Our tariff with the rest of the world does not apply to our northern neighbour. That policy already has driven American manufacturers across the Canadian borders, built vast plants with American capital on Canadian soil, employing Canadian workmen to supply trade, that capital should be kept at home to employ American workingmen to supply Canadian demands. We should admit Canadian wood pulp and Canadian paper free in return for Canada's admitting our agricultural implements, our engines, our pumps and other machinery free. We should freely admit Canadian lumber to American planing mills in return for Canada freely admitting other American manufacturing products to Canadian markets.
Then, we find Senator Sherman saying:
The way to union with Canada is not by hostile legislation; not by acts of retaliation, Mr. ARTHURS.
but by friendly overtures. This union is one of the events that must inevitably come in the future; it will come by the logic of the situation, and no politician or combination of politicians can prevent it. The true policy of this government is to tender freedom in trade and intercourse, and to make this tender in such a fraternal way that it shall be an overture to the Canadian people to become a part of this Republic. . . The settlement of the Northwest territory, the Louisiana and Florida purchases, the annexation of Texas, and the acquisition from Mexico are examples of the adaptation of our form of government for expansion, to absorb and unite, to enrich and build up, to ingraft in our body politic adjacent countries, and while strengthening the older states, confer prosperity and development on the new states admitted into this brotherhood of Republican States. . . With a firm conviction that this consummation most devoutly to be wished is within the womb of destiny, and believing that it is our duty to hasten its coming, I am not willing, for one, to vote for any measure not demanded by national honour that will tend to postpone the good time coming, when the American flag will be the signal and sign ot the union of all the English-speaking peoples of the continent from the Rio Grande to the Arctic ocean.-Senator Sherman in the United States Senate.
I have given you sufficient to show the opinion that the Americans hold as regards the ultimate result of this treaty. There is no question in my mind that the principal aim of the promoters of this treaty on the other side of the line is to divert trade into American channels, gradually to obtain control of Canadian trade, both export and local, and prevent Canada from asking for or receiving a preference from Great Britain. We have had many unsatisfactory experiences in dealing with the United States, and in every case the United States have had the best of the bargain. Only a year ago the United States, through their government, held the big stick over this government, over the same men who negotiated this treaty a few months ago. In passing the Payne-Aldrich treaty at that time it was threatened that they would put an extra duty of 25 per cent on all Canadian goods unless Canada made certain concessions. It is quite true that these concessions did not amount to much but the principle was and is absolutely wrong. We should control our own duties absolutely free from the United States in any way.
There has been absolutely no demand in Canada for this treaty. The people have been and are perfectly satisfied with the conditions as they exist at the present time. There are many electors in past elections, have openly said that there was very little difference between the Conservative and reform parties in so far as their policy was concerned. The Reform party had a platform which was somewhat similar to that of the Conservative party in many respects.

When they came into power in 1896 they practically swallowed the National Policy holus bolus. They kept on the same duties, increased them in some cases and in some cases decreased them a very little. The prosperity of Canada at this present juncture has been entirely owing to the policy put into effect by the Conservatives many years ago.
This idea of tariff stability has been drilled into the people not only by the present opposition-the government at that time- but also by hon. gentlemen who are on the ministerial benches now. I have an extract here from a speech made by the right hon. leader of the government in November, 1910, only a few months ago He said:
The people of the west are now asking for a reduction of duty on certain articles which they consume. That is a very proper subject ot investigation,

Not for any treaty, not for any resolution of this kind, but a proper subject for investigation.
-and we intend to investigate it. But at the proper time.
The hon. gentleman who at the present time is leading the House, the Minister of Finance, in 1906-7, page 287 of Hansard, said:
Our desire has been to encourage a larger degree of tariff stability-not a slavish adherence to every item in the tariff. But we have been desirous that the impression should go abroad that the government were not willing to make changes hastily, that they were rather slow to do anything in that line, and only when a case became of extreme urgency would we undertake to make changes.
Later on he said:
We have, therefore, from time to time resisted many applications for changes, not because in some instances there may not have been something in the argument, but because it was not wise to make changes too often, and if in one or two cases there was some reason perhaps to justify a change I do not think anybody has suffered any serious loss by the delay.
It will be the policy of the government to have that inquiry made throughout the Dominion with the utmost care . . . care will be taken to afford opportunity to every class who wish to present" tlieir views to come and state in what respect they think either that the tariff is right and should he maintained or that it is defective and what changes they believe should be made.
Speaking in another place he said:
When the moment for tariff revision arrives, the public of Canada may rest assured that the government will undertake the work in the spirit of moderation and caution that has prevailed in their past actions in tariff affairs, avoiding the extremes which almost always find advocates, and having regard for
what is best; not for particular industries or particular sections of the country, hut for the interests of the people of the whole of the Dominion.
In another place, also in the year 1906, he said:
Now that we are approaching the question of a general tariff revision, we again wish to keep in mind this idea of tariff stabilty. We do not desire to make radical changes. We feel that the general conditions of Canada today is such that no radical changes in the tariff are called for.
In spite of these declarations the Minister of Finance, on April 6 of this year said in this House:
What we have done is no departure from the policy of Canada; it is in accordance with the policy of Canada for forty years. . .
. . . There is an important difference in the position of the United States government then and now. They were proposing a radical departure from the policy of the country, and they may have needed information of that sort to support their case, but we certainly did not.
They repudiated the promises, such as I have just read, of a tariff commission, and we find the government coming down here with this proposition and asking the country to accept it offhand without any evidence, without any commission, without any knowledge as to the ultimate effect of the agreement, or what effect it will have upon various sections of the country, and we are accused of-I was going to say obstruction -because we do not let this pass without any consideration at all. The Prime Minister at one point said that this was before the country because it was one of the planks of the reform platform of 1893. I thought the reform platform of 1893 was a thing that had passed away long ago but they will revive it once in a while. It may interest some hon. gentlemen to have recalled to their recollection some of the planks of the platform of 1893 which have been allowed to pass into oblivion:
Senate reform.
Reduction of expenditure.
Lower taxation.
Free trade as they have it in England.
These are apparently the principal planks of the platform of 1893.

But, there is some reason for the changed attitude of the government, and in looking around I have come to this conclusion. On November 4 of last year an election was held in the United States at which the democratic, or low tariff party, were successful. They obtained control of the House of representatives and they will, I believe, shortly have control of the Senate of the United States. Mr. Taft, President of the United States, elected by the Republican party, and desirous of a second term as president, looked around for some means by which he could obtain a second term. This bright idea struck him and it is a remarkable thing that on or about the same day an election was held in Canada. One of the strongest constituencies held by this government in the province from which they derive their principal support saw fit to repudiate the government's policy upon a very important issue and the Candidate of the government was defeated in Drummond and Arthabaska, Quebec. These things occurred within a day or two of one another.
I honestly believe that the Prime Minister and the government got cold feet as Mr. Taft did and they looked around for some means to cloud the. issue in the coming elections. That is the reason why the time of parliament has been taken up with this proposition. It is strange that during this long debate the members of the government side of the House have been unable to offer any reason for this policy of theirs. The Minister of Finance, though he spoke eloquently in introducing the motion, gave only one side of the story. He told the farmers of 'Canada about the 90,000,000 market in the United States, but he forgot to tell them that these 90 millions would invade their own home market. He did not tell the farmers of Canada that 80 per cent of their products were sold in Canada so long as the tariff continued to protect them, and he did not prove nor could he prove that the Canadian farmers would continue to sell that 80 per cent in the home market if the treaty came into force. The Minister of Finance also forgot to tell our farmers that 13 other countries as well as the United States would be able to compete with them in their home market. Then, the Minister of Customs took 25 minutes to tell the House of the great benefit Canada would derive from the free exportation of talc. I confess that when the Minister of Customs wras speaking I had a vague idea of what talc was, but I was comforted by knowing that the Minister of Customs knew less about it than I did, because he told us it was something to beautify the complexion, whereas the truth is, that it is commercially used for whitening writing paper. I find, however, from the official returns that there are 27 men in the whole Mr. ARTHURS.
of Canada engaged in the talc industry, and that the averages wages paid them is $1.32 a day, which is less than we pay in Northern Ontario for men who work with the pick and shovel. I honestly believe that the Minister of Customs took up the time of the House talking about talc because he had no better argument to offer. Then again he was very eloquent on the fact that the duty on iron ore exported to the United States was to be reduced by 33J per cent and as the present duty is only 15 cents a ton we are to have me magmn-cent concession of 5 cents on each ton of iron ore. These are samples of the argument put up by the Minister of Customs, one of the very men responsible for this Reciprocity agreement. So far as iron ore is concerned, I believe that the best thing that could happen to Canada would be to absolutely prohibit the exportation of iron ore because I believe it should all be manufactured in this country and until we are able to manufacture it w'e ought to keep it here. The people of Ontario have had a lesson right along this line. For years the Conservative party in that province advocated the prohibition of the exportation of sawlogs, but the Liberal goverment resisted it for years until finally they were compelled to adopt that policy. We were told that if such a law w^ent into force, timber limits would not be worth ten cents a square mile. Well, I know something about timber limits; I know something about the conditions then and now, and I know that from the day the prohibition of the export of sawlogs went into force in Ontario up to the present time the price of timber limits has continued to increase. The result of that policy was that labour was employed in Canada, that our Georgian Bay ports were built up, that the Michigan mills engaged in that industry had to be moved to the Canadian side and that the population of the Georgian Bay towns largely increased. I believe, Sir, that the same would work out in regard to the prohibition of the export of iron ore or any other natural resources of that nature, the Prime Minister, as usual, spoke eloquently in favour of reciprocity, but if you study his speech you will find he said absolutely nothing as to the merits of reciprocity. His sole argument was that Sir John Macdonald or Lord Elgin or some one else said something in favour of reciprocity away back in 1854 or 1879. I am free to confess that I do not care a cent about -what Sir John Macdonald or Lord Elgin or any one else said in 1854, and I do not think the average Canadian elector cares either. But if we are to dip into ancient history we need not go as far back as 1879 or 1854 because we have the utterances of the Prime Minister and of the Minister of Finance of recent date which show that not so long ago they wete adverse

to the policy they aie now promoting. Speaking in 1898 the Prime Minister said:
Canada to-day is not in favour of reciprocity. There was a time when. Canadians, beginning with myself, would have given many things to obtain the American market, but thank heaven these days are past and over.
Ten years afterwards in 1908, speaking at the Imperial Conference the right hon. gentleman said:
There was a time when we were wanting, reciprocity with the United States, but our efforts and our offers were put aside and negatived. We have said good-bye to that trade, ard we now put all our hopes on the British trade.
In 1903, when he was proposing the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill we have this further pronouncement from the right hon. gentleman
Such is our duty, it is immediate and imperative. It is not for to-morrow, but of this day, of this hour and of this minute. Heaven grant that it be not already too late; heaven grant that whilst we tarry and dispute, the trade of Canada is not deviated to other channels, and that an ever vigilant competitor does not take to himself the trade that belongs to those who acknowledge Canada as their native or their adopted land. Upon this question we feel that our position is absolutely safe and secure; we feel that it corresponds to the beating of every Canadian heart. Now, sir, we lay it down as a principle, upon which we are to be judged by friend or foe, that we are to have a transcontinental railway, that its terminus must be in Canadian waters, and that the whole line, every inch of it, must be in Canadian territory. We say further that such a line is a necessity of our commercial indepen 1 ence.
What country had the right hon. gentleman in his mind then?
It was evidently the United States, because his argument could apply to no other nation.

Then, in 1899 the right hon. the Prime Minister said:
If we know the hearts and minds of our people at present, I think I am not making too wide a statement when I say that the general feeling in Canada to-day is not in favour of reciprocity. There was a time when Canadians would have given many things to obtain the American market, there was a time not long ago, when the market of the great cities of the Union was the only Mr-ket we had for any of our products. But thank Heaven, these days are past and over now. We are not dependent upon the American market as we Were at one time.
In that short extract from the speech of the right hon. gentleman lies the true secret of the difference between the period mentioned from 1866 to 1879, and the present time. At that time we had no railroads, we had little or no canals, our farmers Were absolutely dependent on the United States for a market for their products; we had no other market, we could reach no other. But things are entirely changed now. We have spent millions to build up a railway system and to provide the best facilities for transporting our products, so that at the present time Liverpool is a nearer market for the Dominion of Canada than New York.
A few words in regard to the opinions, or the late opinions, of the Minister of Finance, because he has changed them very often. Speaking in 1899 he said:
Whatever our American friends may have intended by their trade policy, there is one thing that they certainly have done; they have made Canadians more independent and. selfreliant and have caused them to look more steadily than before to their home market and to their markets over the sea, where there is an open door. Especially have our producers given attention to the British market during the past two years, when our trade relations with the mother country have been so developed and increased by the preferential tariff. Therefore, the market of our friends to the south of us is much less important to us than it was a few years ago, and we are better able to do without reciprocity than we have been at any previous time in the history of Canada.
That is the hon. the Minister of Finance.

The same man, one of them. In 1906, speaking on the Budget, the Minister of Finance said:
The farmer, as a rule, is a low tariff man; but if you ask him whether he wants the duties on agricultural products abolished, he is apt to be a little careful. Some will say yes and others, no. Others will say: Take the duties off agricultural products if you take them off everything else. Well, whenever we have made changes in the schedule of agricultural duties, as a rule they are in the direction of a little increase. We do not want the farmer to say that the changes made are to the disadvantage of the things he himself produces. In fact some farmers are strong advocates of high duties although the general tendency is the other way. Therefore we have not made any changes, and any we have made are in the way of an increase to some extent.
In spite of all these pledges given by different members of the government at different times, the government say they have pledged the honour of Canada to press this measure through parliament without delay-no investigation into prices in Canada, no report on prices in the United States as compared with Canadian prices, no report on the cost of the production of agricultural products in the 12 other coun-

tries whose product under this agreement can come into direct competition with our own in our own home markets. On this account alone I contend that we on this side of the House are justified in opposing by every lawful means the passage of this reciprocity agreement. If the agreement is a good one, it should not be difficult to prove it by a tariff commission and by a full statement of the surrounding facts, and all these facts should be available not only to every member of this House, but to every elector of Canada.
As an example of how unreliable the information sent out by this government is, I would point out that according to Part II of the Canadian Trade Report for the year 1910, Canada imported from the United States last year $12,070,881 worth of dutiable wheat. Now, I would just like to ask the Minister of Customs if he believes that himself.

I have already referred to the other countries that would come under this agreement without granting to Canada any compensating advantage. We find that Russia, Argentina, Austria-Hungary, Bolivia, Colombia, Denmark, Japan, Norway, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and most of the British colonies, including Australia and New Zealand, would enjoy all the benefits of this agreement, the free access of their agricultural products to the markets of Canada, and we could not send one dollar's worth to them without paying heavy duties. Speakers on the other side of the House make very light of this question, and say it does not amount to very much any way. ^r Quote some of the principal exports of these countries. Denmark, during the year ending December 31, 1909, shipped 196,639,220 pounds of butter of a value of $48,320,668. She shipped upwards of $31,000,000 worth of meat, Australia shipped over $15,000,000 worth of meat, and over $11,600,000 of butter. New Zealand shipped $18 000,000 worth of meat, $8,000,000 worth of butter, and $6,000,000 worth of cheese. Argentine shipped upwards of $40,000,000 worth of meat alone and about $1,500,000 worth of butter, and so on. This shows that these countries are actual shippers to the markets of the world. Then it costs just as little to send a pound of meat frqjn Argentine to Halifax as to send it to Liverpool and meat can be delivered in Mon-

For instance if we wished to ship wheat to France we would have to pay $3.51 a hundred pounds duty, and on lambs 77 cents each. On wheat we have to pay 61.4 cents per hundred pounds, and on barley 26.3 cents a hundred pounds, on potatoes 3.5 cents a hundred pounds, and on butter 2.63 cents per hundred pounds. 11 we wish to ship to Italy we would have to pay on caitle an average duty oi over $6 per head; on wheat 65.80 cents per hundred pounds. I wish to point out that the abrogation of the old reciprocity treaty of 1854-1856 was a blessing in disguise for Canada, although the Americans abrogated it with the intention of driving Canada into annexation or starvation according to their newspapers. It is true that during the term of that treaty Canada enjoyed a short period of prosperity, but I would point out that during the earlier years of its existence the Crimean war was at its height, and prices reached a level not reached since at any time. Shortly after the close of this war, the American war occurred beginning in 1861. and ending in 1865. In 1866, the year after the close of the war, American conditions having become normal, the treaty was abrogated by the United States, and Canada was told that she would be forced into annexation or starvation. It is quite true that Canada at that time was in pretty bad shape, but it was probably the best thing that ever happened to Canada as a whole, and I firmly believe that had it not been for the abrogation of the treaty in 1866 the federation of Canada would bo still in the distant future. Canada was driven to fall back on her own resources. The men who were then at the head of affairs in Canada, some Conservatives and some Reformers, were forced to consult together, and to devise some means whereby we could trade with one another, benefiting one another instead of being scattered provinces as we were at that time. The building of the Intercolonial railway and the Canadian Pacific railway, the acquisition of the northwest territories by Can-Mr. ARTHURS.
ada are, I believe, directly attributable to the abrogation of that treaty, and our prosperity from that time to the present, has been through that means. We have hundreds of millions of dollars in building the various railways and canals. The cost to Canada as a whole has probably exceeded $600,000,000. We have, according to our Reform friends, spent many millions buikh ing up industries. They have now arrived at a stage where they are practically selfsupporting, and yet we would apparently be willing to cast away all these- advantages to go back to the condition of affairs which existed in 1886, and depend almost entirely, because that is what it amounts to in the end, on the market of the United States.	-
I believe that this treaty or agreement, if it does what is claimed for it by its friends, must inevitably lead to the loss of our commercial independence, and ultimately to annexation to the United States. The fact that some hon. gentlemen opposite are acting in good faith, and do not see any danger does not prove that that dangei does not exist. The man who rocks the boat never sees any danger, and the gun that is not loaded is always the most dangerous. I believe that we should look into this matter more thoroughly, that we should have more time, and that the whole thing should be placed in the hands of an independent commission, a commission of business men, who would discuss it thoroughly among themselves, and bring before parliament a finding which, I believe, would be acceptable to the people of Canada.
I believe it would be wise to postpone this treaty untl the Americans have formally settled their tariff matters and until the people of Canada have had an opportunity to thoroughly digest the proposal. As far as I am personally concerned, as I said in the first place, I believe we have no mandate from the people to pass a matter of this kind or to accept such a treaty as is proposed. I believe that in all these great changes the people should be consulted before anything is done. X am prepared to vote against the resolution and to do anything that lies in my power to defeat it until the people have been consulted. If the people say they are prepared to stand behind the agreement my opposition must necessarily cease, and will cease. But I believe that the true solution of the whole question would be an independent commission. We have got along for fifteen or twenty years very well without reciprocity, and I think we can get along for fifteen or twenty years more without it just as well. I believe the people should have a true statement of the facts. Let the whole matter be laid before the people; let them have an opportunity to form an independent judgment,

and they will come to a wise and independent decision. And I believe their verdict will be that the best course is to allow Canada to go on as in the past and to work out her destiny as part of the British empire with independent control of her own affairs.

speechtext:
If I am forced to proceed, of course, I will proceed, but I think this demand upon me will be recognized by the people I represent as a most extraordinary one, I would call the attention of the First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson)-who seems to regard this as a joke, but I can assure him that the people I represent do not at all regard as a joke the change he proposes to inflict upon us-to the fact that the Minister from Victoria, British Columbia (Mr. Templeman) is not present, and it seems to me he should be present while the interests of his province are under discussion. The only other member from British Columbia on the government side of the House who has taken part in this discussion is not present. And I think it is unfair to him and to us to ask us to discuss here the statements he has made while he is not here to take his part in the discussion. But, meanwhile there are some subjects which can be laid before the House at the present time with which these hon. gentlemen are not very immediately concerned, but to which it would seem to be advantageous for them to give attention. I have a very valuable text here which should afford food for thought on the part of every member of this House.' It is in the shape of a pamphlet prepared by the Canadian National League and going very fully into this subject. A good many members of the House, no doubt, are familiar with the origin of this Canadian National League and with the literature which it has put out. Hon. members will recall that when this matter
of reciprocity was sprung upon the country no persons were more shocked at the attitude of the government and what was generally regarded as the folly of our ambassadors extraordinary to Washington than were some of the men who, up to that time, had been in the front ranks of the Liberal party in Canada. We found this feeling taking shape in Toronto in a manifesto signed by no less than eighteen leaders of the Liberal party at that important centre, eighteen prominent members of the Liberal party who thought it worth while to declare to the public that this action on the part of the government had finished them with the Liberal party, that they could no longer assist in perpetuating the reign of a government that had proved so false to every principle which it would have led its supporters to believe it professed, that had proven recreant to its duty to the people and that had so shamelessly, I may say, betrayed the trust conferred upon it. So, we have these eighteen Liberals promoting the formation of the Canadian National League and taking part in the dissemination of literature to show the people of Canada precisely what this arrangement means to us. The object of the league is stated in their prospectus:
To oppose the adoption of the proposed Reciprocity Agreement between Canada and the United States of America and to support such measures as will uphold Canadian nationality and British connection, will preserve our fiscal independence and will continue to develop our present national policy of interprovincial and external trade, under which the Dominion has achieved its present prosperity
The basis on which the league has been
formed is: Canadian nationality, British connection and fiscal independence.
Three objects which I am sure must commend themselves to every man in this House, objects worthy of the position which these gentlemen have occupied up. to the present in the ranks of the Liberal party of Canada. The league declares that it is non-partizan in character, that it is opposed to the Laurier government because it believes that in negotiating this agreement with the United States and in endeavouring to have it adopted by parliament, the government is not upholding Canadian nationality and British connection, and is not preserving our fiscal independence. They would be opposed to any government, whether Liberal or Conservative for the same reason, and so I am convinced will the great majority of the electors of Canada oppose any government, whether Liberal or Conservative, which proposes to surrender to the United States our fiscal independence. While opposed to this agreement for the reasons stated, they are opposed to it on patriotic grounds also, because they sav:

We believe that our government failed to appreciate properly the present position and condition of Canada, contrasted with its position land condition when reciprocity would have been welcomed, and that it lost sight of the fact that the principles underlying its own policy for years past are utterly inconsistent with the principles underlying this agreement.
In the present pamphlets, and in those to follow, nothing will be said intentionally to wound the feelings of any one, and no offensive personal allusions will be made. The subject is above party and persons, and will be so kept and treated.
Of this fact we have seen tonight the most convincing evidence read by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Arthurs), evidence which fully justifies the position taken by the league.
The opposition will be kept up until the people have pronounced upon the question.
Until we have the opportunity we desire of going to the polls, and putting before the people of Canada the question whether they wish for a reciprocal arrangement of this kind, or whether they are content to be bludgeoned by any government in continuing this debate with the idea of forcing this House to consent to something which they would never consent to willingly. This league takes as its first text fihe significant statement of the President of the United States that Canada is at the parting of the ways, and it submits evidence to show that this statement is unfortunately only too true. As this pamphlet says:
Shall we continue along the path which has led us to our present prosperity and to our proud position as the keystone in the arch of a united British Empire; or, shall we take the path that leads to Washington?
Facts which indicates the answer which should be made to this question are set forth in this pamphlet.
When the Hon. Mr. Fielding announced to parliament the reciprocity agreement he alleged, as the chief reason for making it, that ever since confederation Canada has been committed to the policy embodied in the agreement, and earnestly desires it at the present time, that the Conservative party, as well as the Liberal party, was committed to it. He did not attempt, by facts and figures, to prove that upon economic grounds it would he beneficial to Canada; he assumed that it would be so.
Now Mr. Chairman, I would like to call your attention to the fact that not only is the statement true made hy these protesting Liberals that the hon. gentlemen who arranged this agreement have presented to the house no satisfactory reasons why we should adopt it, but that their failure to do so has been accentuated by the extraordinary course of their followers

in parliament who are content to sit still and swallow this, as they have swallowed every other nauseous dose presented to them while they have occupied their present benches.
An examination of the pages of history shows the damaging effect of this arrangement. It is recalled to us how reciprocity damaged the St. Lawrence exports .
From 1854 to 1866 a reciprocity treaty existed between the old province of Canada and the United States of America. This province at that time comprised only Upper Canada and Lower Canada (now Ontario and Quebec). Confederation did not take place till Julv 1st, 1867.
When this treaty was made the province of Canada had a population of approximately 2,100,000; when the treaty was abrogated it had increased to about 2,650,000. Settlement had extended hut a few miles, comparatively, north of the United States boundary in either Upper Canada or Lower Canada. The Grand Trunk railway from Toronto to Montreal was the only railway connecting the two provinces. The Great Western railway from Niagara to Windsor (now part of the Grand Trunk) was the only railway running through Ontario's western peninsula. There were no large factories, and but a small home market, while the population of the United States in 1851 was 26,500,000, and in 1866 it was 36,000,000. Communication across the Atlantic was meagre and expensive.
Showing that under the former reciprocity arrangement the population of the United States made the extraordinary increase, notwithstanding the disturbance of the war of secession, in four years, from 26 millions to 36 millions; while Canada, which, we are told, should benefit so much by reciprocity, made the insignificant increase of from 2,100,000 to 2,600,000. Now Mr. Chairman, I would like once more to call attention to the fact that the minister representing British Columbia in this gov-vernment is not in his place. I protest that it is unfair for the government to force the members from British Columbia to continue this debate when the minister representing that province teels himself physically unfit to occupy his place in the chamber. I say that in a matter of this kind there should not be one rule for a minister and one rule for a private member, that it is a rank injustice to me that after a six days' trip on the train I should be asked to speak now while the minister from my province, the man who, with his colleagues, proposes to saddle this burden upon us, is reposing in his bed. I would ask the government again whether they cannot produce here the body of the Min-nister of Inland Revenue or else consent to adjourm Mr. Chairman. I would ask the first minister or any of his colleagues to say whether they do not think it is a reasonable request that when a matter

of this kind is being discussed of such great interest to our province the minister from that province should at least be present.

Now, to resume, if any of those hon. gentlemen who are making those remarks on the other side of the House wish to get on the floor for a while I will have much pleasure in yielding it to them. If they have not the courage to stand up and occupy the floor I would ask that they observe the rules of the House and not make what they intend to be disconcerting remarks disturbing to the trend of thought that I am applying to this discussion. We are led to believe from a study of the results of the reciprocity arrangement of 1854-66 that its effect upon the east and west traffic was a warning which should be a lesson to us. Here are some of the results. The House will pardon me if I spend some time in reading because it is impossible for a man to carry in his head the number of valuable figures which I propose to present during the course of my argument:
Following the treaty, business in and out of the port of Montreal declined.
I would commend that to the consideration of those hon. gentlemen now representing the city of Montreal, who, without giving any reason at all for the faith that is in them, propose voting for this agreement for no other reason than that it is presented to them by the government which is their master.
The carrying trade of the St. Lawrence in 1854 was valued at $33,633,128. In the next year it dropped to $15,208,600.
That is it had shrunk to less than fifty per cent of what it had been before.
The ships' tonnage going to the sea from Montreal and Quebec decreased from 1,487,097 to 870,794 tons, and the value of the exports from $42,000,000 to $28,000,000. On Canadian canals in the first year of the treaty the tolls fell off by 32 per cent.
An examination shows that there was an advance in the price of farm products.
This advance we have often heard of during the course of this discussion, but
it was not entirely, or even to a large extent, due to this treaty with the United States:
The Crimean war . . . began in 1854 and continued during 1855 and 1856, and the price of food stuffs in Europe increased rapidly and persistently-wheat in England went up to $2.50 per bushel. When peace was made, prices fell, until the Civil War in the United States broke out. From 1860 to 1865, because of this war, farming in the United States w'as considerably curtailed, and the market for Calnadian products was correspondingly enlarged.
This in a large measure, if not entirely, accounts for what increase did take place in the prices of Canadian commodities during that period. But no sooner was the war over than a demand arose in the United States for the abrogation of the treaty which some farmers, through jealousy, thought was conferring some benefit upon their Canadian neighbours. This demand was not only from the farmers, but, as on the present occasion, trade relations with Canada were made a foot-ball by the politicians of the United States who entered upon a political cry for the termination of the arrangement, so that by pursuing Canada with a hostile tariff policy they might drive her into closer political relations with them if not indeed into annexation.
In 1866 the United States put up the tariff wall again, and the Canadian farmer was worse off than ever.
The existence of the reciprocity treaty had disarranged the channels of trade just as the adoption of the arrangement or pact now before the House would disarrange all our avenues of trade. Having ceased to look to the British market in the endeavour to cultivate that of their nearer neighbour, Canadian producers had come to rely almost entirely on the United States market. They were sending everything they could across the boundary and impoverishing their land and capital. They received many warnings that they might be shut out of the market which they were told was to be for them a continuous and continuing blessing. Many of them.thought that they were ruined for life and a decided leaning towards annexation arose in many minds. This is the record from history. It is not the vain prophecy of any person attempting to frighten his fellow citizens into opposing something which otherwise they might be inclined to try. But we have the lesson from history that many Canadians were so fearful of the consequences of the abrogation of this treaty that a decided leaning towards annexation with the United States arose in many minds. When we draw this lesson from history it cannot be, said that we are reflecting in any sense upon the Canadians of that day. It is not

regarded as a reflection upon a Canadian or a British subject from the old country, that when he goes to the United States and takes up his residence there, he shortly after takes the oath of allegiance to the American Republic and forswears his allegiance to the British Empire.
That is done by the most loyal of British subjects as a measure of self-protection. Haying gone to the United States to make their jiving there, it would 'be unfair to themselves, it would be unfair to their famines, to persist for a sentimental reason in remaining apart from the people amongst whom they made their living. As with these individuals so it may well be with the Dominion or with a province of Canada. Thus if by an alliance of this kind with the United States we hopelessly commit our trade arrangements to their hands, the time may come when they will be in a position to put such pressure on us that it may become an issue with us as a nation whether we shall do what so many citizens, quite our equals in loyalty to the British Empire, are forced to do as individuals. I commend that to the consideration of these gentlemen, who, when they say anything at all upon this subject, are fond of sneering at what they call the waving of the old flag and professions of lip-loyalty. I ask them whether they see any reason why we as a community should not be proof against what our equals, who have gone to the United States from England, instead of coming first to Canada, have been unable to resist as individuals. I for one do not wish to take the risk; I do not wish to defy the lightning, but while I have a chance I would prefer to take precautions against being struck.
The abrogation of the treaty was a blessing in disguise. It stopped the fatal drain of fertility from the soil. At the very time the movement for confederation was fructifying, it turned the Canadian people once more to the British market, which had grown enormously through the expansion of trade in manufactured goods all over the world.
We were referred early in this discussion to the lectures delivered under the auspices of the Minister of Agriculture-who, also I regret to say is not in the House-in which the people of the Province of Quebec were warned that it was the most disastrous kind of farming to export hay, instead of Taismg cattle and enriching the land. Up to the time the minister had started this crusade the farmers of Quebec had been exporting to the United States this hay which they should have fed to the cattle on their own farms. A similar state of ai?a*rs	during the continuance of
the Reciprocity Treaty of 1854 and we are told that the abrogation of the Treaty stopped the fatal drain of fertility from the soil.	|

And now, as a parting gift to the province which has kept them in power this government proposes to facilitate the export of hay. I ask them if they have no higher regard for the interest of that province than to attempt to prolong their term in office by a catch-cry such as reciprocity, upon which they hope to be judged in a rush by the people, to the exclusion of all the sins which otherwise would have been arrayed against them, and as to which they fear condemnation from their fellow-citizens in Quebec as well as their fellow-citizens in the other provinces. The Jfrime Minister laughs.
Sir WILFRID LAUR1ER. Hear, hear.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has no fear of the consequences. He has adopted the motto of his distinguished predecessor who said 'After me the deluge.' The Prime Minister laughs, and provided he can persuade his people to give him another term in office it is a matter of indifference to him how many years of repentance will follow their sad experience.
In 1867 confederation came, and with dt the hope which had previously been confined to a few ardent patriots-that Canada would become a nation within a nation, and would work out her destiny as such-spread to the mass of our people; and there and then began one of the most courageous and difficult and patriotic enterprises which has ever been witnessed, viz.: the building up upon half a continent, by a handful of people, of a great Dominion, and the overcoming of enormous natural difficulties and disadvantages.
Consider, for a moment, the difficulties to be overcome. The British North America Act, Canada's constitution, first united Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and provided for the union of Prince Edward Island and British Columbia and the vast territories between British Columbia and Hudson bay and extending from the United States boundary to the Arctic ocean. Canada's task was to weld all these into one Dominion and to provide for its government, and to preserve its autonomy and British connection.
The first part of the task has been accomplished. The great territories referred to were added, and the province of Manitoba was formed on the 15th of July, 1870. British Columbia came in on the 20th of July, 1871, and Prince Edward Island on the 1st of July, 1873. This first part was comparatively easy.
These were the days when there began to arise in Canada the feeling that we should renew our relationship with the United States our only near neighbours, and that it might be more profitable to us, than to attempt to establish connection with the scattered provinces of Canada across the great gaps then existing. While the people of Nova Scotia for instance, the province represented toy the hon. gentleman respon-

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.

speechtext:
sible for this pact, were still lamenting to a large degree their union with Canada- and if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) was doing anything at all at that time no doubt he was helping to voice the plaint of their union with Canada and to satisfy them then as he would satisfy them now that it was more to their profit to trade with the United States than to trade with their sister provinces in the newly formed Dominion. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) will excuse me for saying so, it is one of the most sinister features in connection with it, and tends to induce the people of Canada to regard it with suspicion, to regard it as recommended to them, not by one who has at heart the welfare of Canada, but one, who hopelessly biassed as to the impossibility of a happy union of his province with the rest of Canada, would like to round off his career by showing that he has been right all his life, and that those of us having more "hope, greater courage, greater confidence in our ability as Canadians to make all the provinces benefit from the union, have been wrong in our contention of all these years, that we are happier as a united people trading east and west, than we would have been had we followed the advice of the Minister of Finance and his friends in Nova Scotia, and had cut adrift from Canada and continued to trade as before on the best terms his province could arrange with the United States.
The House will pardon me, I hope, if I do not speak with utmost fluency on this occasion, because, while I hope to proceed for a very long time yet on this very interesting subject, as I would be loath to drop it without doing.justice to it, yet it is not conducive to eloquence of ideas or fluency of diction to speak after travelling across the continent-to be called upon to speak up to midnight or afterwards on the very day one has accomplished this journey of
3,000	miles.
I was referring to how nature has favoured trade between the north and the south', and how the fathers of confederation, of whom there are none in this House, had attempted to introduce the east and west principle. While we have never heard much in support of that principle from the hon. Minister of Finance, the right hon. the First Minister has taken a much larger view of the country in which he has risen, and deservedly risen, to so high an eminence, and has at times striven to do the very opposite of what this legislation of his would perform; he has striven to the best of his abilities to develop the east and west principle in Canadian trade. What Canada has accomplished in this direction so far has been accomplished because reciprocity with the United States has not existed Canada could not have accomplished this
had reciprocity been in force. The lessons of history enable us to speak with certainty as to the past, while we can only predict the future. This prediction, however, voiced by the best people in Canada after the most careful consideration, is that the result of the proposed reciprocity agreement will be to check the growth and development of the east and west trade, and the trade between Canada and 'Great Britain, to weaken our British connection, and to render our task of consolidating the scattered provinces of the dominion and preserving our fiscal independence and autonomy, much more difficult. I would like to call the attention of hon, gentlemen opposite to a statement made by their late colleagues, the 18 prominent Liberals who signed the manifesto to which I referred at the beginning of my remarks. These gentlemen are not Tory politicians aching for office; they are not waving the old flag or shouting loyalty because of any affection for the Tory party or because of any desire to put any other party out of power in Canada. They must be credited "with speaking the sentiments of their hearts, as representing the best thought in the Liberal party, the thought that we confidently hope to see indicated when the people get a chance to pronounce on this subject. These gentlemen, speaking in advance of their fellow Liberals who have not yet been heard, said:
We believe that, this reciprocity arrangement will eventually result in our losing our autonomy and in becoming politically a part of the American Union. We are aware that opinions honestly differ on the points; but we ask, why take the risk?
A pertinent question, Mr. Chairman: why take the risk? I am very sorry that our minister from British Columbia is so little interested in this subject that he is not present, that if a messenger was sent for him, he has not been able to get him away from his couch; because I would like to recall to him in this connection what occurred in my own little city only a couple of weeks ago. The pertinent question asked in this pamphlet reminds me of it. Our minister was spellbinding in British Columbia, and the gentlemen on the other side who have been so often thrilled with his eloquence in this House will realize with what tremors we witnessed his approach on our several constituencies. However, we could not control his movements, as we cannqt control them now. He was accompanied by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clarke), to whom the unfortunate fact that he is still engaged in his patriotic mission and is also absent from his place in this House. The hon. minister was a little unequal to the task set before him in the riding of New Westminster. The First

Minister I know admires that riding, because we gave him a great welcome there last year, and he was pleased to speak with his customary eloquence in the kindest and most flattering terms of the progress he had observed in New Westminster. 1 am sure he had a high opinion of the intelligence of the people of that district, except that he might regard it as a blot on their intelligence that they made the unfortunate choice of their representative at the last election; so he will realize that there was not much encouragement for these two federal spellbinders without drawing in the unwilling services of the deposed leader of the Liberals in British Columbia, tne gentleman who for so many years represented tne district in the legislature and who, no doubt, would at the present moment be a candidate for election to this House were it not that he recognizes that this arrangement makes the prospect of the election of any Liberal there altogether hopeless.
This gentleman, Mr. John Oliver, a farmer, possibly the best informed man in the whole district as to conditions in the district was brought forward to give the best comfort he could to the two spell binders from Ottawa and the best he could say for them was this, that he was losing no sleep because of the issue of reciprocity. It was a matter of indifference to him, the chief witness they could produce from the district, whether or not this reciprocity campaign succeeded, because, he said, we are too prosperous to be affected by it. He said the farmers of this district were never in their history so prosperous, so happy and so contented as they are to-day, and supplementing what he said, I ask with these pamphleteers, why take the risk? That question can produce only one answer from the farmers of the district of New Westminster, from the farmers throughout the length and breadth of British Columbia who see the livelihood of themselves and their families menaced by the proposition, that they shall be delivered over to their comparatively poverty-stricken neighbours across the American boundary. Why take the risk? and echo answers, why? There is no other answer in this House or out of it, except that in a moment of panic the Finance Minister of Canada promised President Taft that if President Taft would forbear imposing the American surtax on Canadian products he would go down representing this government and make the .surrender in which we are now asked to assist.
Reviewing the history of the position of affairs we find that the British North America Act, by section 145, declared that the Intercolonial railway was essential to the consolidation of the union of British North America. This principle of east and west transportation ran through the agreement with British Columbia for it was made an Mr. TAYLOR (New Westminster!
essential part of the union that the Canadian Pacific Railway should be built. And here it is opportune to say that British Columbia had, before the time of her union with Canada, ample experience of free trade with the United States to settle her in advance in opposition to the arrangement now before us. These pioneers of British Columbia who know by their own experience or by what they have heard from their fathers of the results up to 1871 need no other argument than the lesson of their own history for their present opposition and hostility to this arrangement. We had at that time in British Columbia a system of free ports, the idea being that if we could produce the wares of the world free of duty at the ports of Victoria and Nanaimo these ports would develop into great trade centres and would become very great entrepots of commerce. In a way that worked well but it was soon realized that since everything grown'in the United States would come into these two thriving Canadian settlements and that nothing grown on Vancouver Island, then the centre of population of British Columbia, could be admitted to the United States, the whole settlement was drawn over to the American side, and after the Island had become depopulated as a result of the experiment, the people decided that they would depart from their position of isolation from the rest of Canada, that they would invite Canada to make terms of union with them, that they would cease their efforts to trade north and south as this government now invites them to do again, and would begin to develop trade east and west with their fellow-Britishers in the Dominion of Canada. So there came about the union of British Columbia with the rest of Canada. I referred to the help given by the First Minister for a long time in developing this east and west trade. I am reminded that this principle more strongly than ever before, actuated the Laurier government when they committed this parliament and this country to the gigantic task of building the Grand Trunk Pacific and National Transcontinental railway. Upon that occasion Sir Wilfrid said to the House of Commons:
A railway to extend from the shores of the Atlantic ocean to the shores of the Pacific ocean, and to be, every inch of it, on Canadian soil, is a national as well as a commercial necessity. That such a road must he built, that it is, in the language which I have used, a natiolnal and commercial necessity, that it is a corollary of our status as a nation, that it is a requisite of our commercial development is a proposition to which, up to this moment, I have heard no dissent. . [DOT] [DOT] We consider -that it is the duty of all those who -sit within these walls by the will of the people, to provide immediate means whereby the products of those new settlers may find an exit to the ocean at the least possible cost, and whereby, likewise, a market may be

found in this new region for those who toil in the forests, in the fields, in the mines, in the shops of the older provinces. Such is our duty; it is immediate and imperative. It is not for to-morrow, but of this day, of this hour and of this minute.
Let me interrupt the reading of the right hon. gentleman's eloquent words to point out that while we were warned of the momentous necessity of the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific, while it was not for to-morrow, but of this day and of this hour and of this minute, a pressing and imperative duty on the community, in which we could brook no delay in the construction of this road, and the investment of $200,000,000 in its construction, up to this time the road has failed to accomplish its purpose in any degree, it is not yet finished and the construction of the British Columbia portion of it has barely commenced. It therefore seems to me a most extraordinary thing that, having committed us to an expense of $200,000,000 in order to promote the patriotic principle of trade between east and west, the right hon. gentleman should be found apparently forgetting the principles which animated him at that time, and asking us to forget that it is our patriotic duty to encourage trade between east and west; inviting us to send our trade south to Washington, Oregon and California and to draw north from those states the trade which we would so willingly draw from Saskatchewan and Alberta into British Columbia. However, I have been digressing. I trust, Mr Chairman, that you and the Committee will pardon the digression and will not take it amiss that this interruption has taken place in reading the eloquent remarks of the right honorable the first minister. The right hon. gentleman invoked Divine assistance:
Heaven grant that it he not already too late; heaven grant that whilst we tarry and dispute, the trade of Canada is not deviated to other channels, and that an ever vigilant competitor does not take to himself the trade that properly belongs to those who acknowledge Canada as their native or their adopted land.
Was the right hon. gentleman mistaken when he assumed, as he then did assume, that he was a favourite of Providence, that Heaven had granted his prayer even before it was uttered, and that his influence had been such that this calamity had been averted? What are we to think of the pressure which must have been put upon the night hon. gentleman by his colleagues returning from Washington when he was induced to adopt the proposition they brought, notwithstanding the record that he had addressed the House in this language, that he had warned us against the folly of doing that very thing to which they say thev have committed what they
call the honour of Canada. But I say the honour of Canada is not so committed. When two ministers so far forget the duties they owe to Canada, and the responsibility of their office, as to take upon themselves to abandon the principles of their party, to betray their leader, to offer to a foreign and dangerous competitor freedom in our markets which we cannot enjoy in theirs, -I say that when two ministers make a promise of that kind they do not pledge the honour of their country. And I am astonished that a man so astute as the Prime Minister did not do what he had the courage to do in other cases when his colleagues made mistakes-tell them that their connection with the government must forthwith cease. I have been looking at the right hon. gentleman in the hope that he might commit himself, if no more than by an involuntary nod of approval. I am sorry to say I have not seen it, but I am quite sure that in his heart he does feel that that course would have been the course of wisdom and that if he had adopted that course it would not have been necessary for him to adopt, as we are told by the chief party organ he has had to adopt as his rallying cry for the next campaign, a motto which, perhaps is misconstrued in the 'Globe' and which it seems to me might be more fittingly put, 'follow where the white feather leads.' Some hon. gentlemen asked me what it says, I wish I had the 'Globe' here; it puts it more precisely and significantly than I can remember it. But it says we are likely to have in the ensuing election as a substitute for the rallying cry 'Let Laurier finish his work' the motto 'Follow where the white plume leads.' Everybody knows that a plume is a feather. I think it would be proper therefore to say 'follow where the white feather leads.' For, if ever there was a white feather brigade in Canadian' politics we have it in these men who have no argument except political force to advance against the reasons laid before the House by hon. members on this side. Now, I am happier than I was, because I have brought a smile to the countenance of the Prime Minister. The right hon. gentleman was not the only one who wished to build up Canada from east to west at the time of the proposal of the Transcontinental Railway. He had sufficient force to draw with him one who must have been in his heart an unwilling colleague. A significant heading in the pamphlet to which I have referred reads, ' Mr. Fielding for another transcontinental.' It says that Mr. Fielding was equally emphatic as the Prime Minister in his declaration of the prinicple that our trade must be built up from east to west. Hon. members who are familiar with the history of the Finance Minister will realize what an effort it must

have been on his part and will realize also what pressure must have been brought upon him by circumstances and his right hon. leader. Perhaps it was upon the principle of tit for tat that he was able on this next occasion to lead his leader. I do not expect however, to learn the mysteries of that Council chamber where, as one of the right hon. Prime Minister's distingushed colleagues once remarked they continue to ' fight like blazes.'
I am glad that there is a fairly good congregation present of hon. gentlemen opposite-even though the minister from British Columbia is not among them-and would call their special attention to these remarks of the Minister of Finance, and would ask them to realize what they mean. He says:
It is desirable that we should give our American. brethren to understand that Canada is resolved to work out her independence in these things, that the present proposal will promote this object, and that even if still another railway should he necessary We shall be prepared to construct it.
Now, if I may be permitted to destroy the continuity of this splendid confession of * new faith on the part of the Finance Minister, I would like to remind him that his first railway has not yet been finished. It is true that he has consented to the construction of a second railway to foster the underlying principle of trade between the east and the west. But while he has placed on this country so huge a burden to promote trade between the east and the west, he comes do this House, forgetting, or ignoring, or not deigning to explain, why the conditions of six or seven years ago are so different from the conditions of today, and tells us that these railways are a mistake, that what we want is not railways between the east and the west, but a new chain of railways to carry the trade of Canada north and south, away from its natural channels, for the benefit of our grasping neighbours in the United States. I will read the. rest of that confession of new faith of the Finance Minister:
Tbe attitude that the government has taken upon tbe subject has already attracted much attention across tbe border, and there is much keener appreciation of Canada's independence than ever before. I
I wonder who told him that. I wonder if he had a private communication from President Taft which inspired him to use this language. I wonder if, since he realized the keenness of the American appreciation of Canadian progress without American assistance, it would not have been logical for him to think that it would be a good idea for Canada to proceed on the course which, according to his own statement, had aroused the admiration of our neighbours to the south. I wonder if it Mr. TAYLOR (New Westminster).
did not show a lack of perspicacity on his part that he did not resist the appeal from Washington to walk into the spiders web which the shrewder politicians of the United States had set for him. Now, to show that these gentlemen were in earnest at the time of the projection of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, I would refer to the steps which they took to ensure that the views they laid before the House might be carried out. In the agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific railway there is this provision in section 42:
It is hereby declared and agreed between tbe parties to this agreement that the aid herein provided for is granted by the government of Canada for the express purpose of encouraging the transportation of goods through Canadian channels.
' Of encouraging the transportation of goods through Canadian channels.'
The company accepts the aid on these conditions, and agrees that all freight originating, on the line of the railway or its branches, not *specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall, when destined for points in Canada, be carried entirely on Canadian territory, or between Canadian inland ports, and that 1_fie through rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall at no time be greater via Canadian ports tlmu via United States ports, and that such traffic, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall be carried to tbe Canadian ocean ports.
This, Mr. Chairman, shows an intention,, at least, to make an arrangement with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company that would secure for Canada the maximum benefit from the construction of that railway, but what are the conditions now? As is recognized everywhere, the main trade to be carried over the Grand Trunk Pacific is the grain trade of the Northwest. Eliminate that and you have no justification, either for the Grand Trunk Pacific or for the succeeding railway indicated by the Finance Minister at that time, and since realized by the bonusing of the Canadian Northern. Now what becomes of all these arguments with respect to the necessity of this railway to carry this grain east and west, to export it by our Pacific ports on one hand, and by Fort William and Port Arthur on the other? The hon. gentlemen now propose the diversion of that traffic from our own heavily bonused railways to the ports of the United States. I would like the House to consider another aspect of this arrangement in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. As they well know, there is a very general suspicion that if there were any possibility of doing it the whole burden of the Grand Trunk Pacific would be shifted to the shoulders of the Canadian people by the philanthropic gentlemen who have projected it for the

benefit of the nation. Now if ever there was a provocation to them to raise any quibble as to their payments promised to Canada, that provocation is supplied by the action of the government, taken even before the completion of the road, tending to destroy all the trade which it was intended should earn for the road the money to pay its obligations to Canada.
It seems to me that this is a subject as to which these ministers should deign to say something to the House, for surely this phase of the case impressed itself upon the cabinet when it was considering this arrangement with the United States evein though, as we have been told, it was put through, for better or for worse, in about the time that it takes to perform a marriage ceremony. It would seem that they should have thought of the momentous effect this diversion of trade would have upon their agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, that they should have realized that it would of a certainty have the effect of saddling upon Canada not only the enormous burden which we have assumed in that connection, but the whole burden of the enterprise. That is a subject which might very well be discussed for a day by itself, as to which I feel wholly unequal at this late hour when the hands of the clock stand at midnight. However, no doubt, before this debate finishes, we will hear from some hon. gentleman on the ministerial benches their views of this aspect of the case, their statement as to the liability, if any, which they expect to have to assume towards the Grand Trunk Railway Company because of the breach of contract and of faith involved in diverting the trade from that road.
Nowt, as I said at the outset, there are matters connected with this arrangement affecting the province of British Columbia which I have not touched upon so far, and which I do not desire to touch upon until the minister from that province is in his place in the House. Unless my failure to come up to the standard of parliamentary oratory under the painful circumstances surrounding my speaking to-night has so annoyed hon. members that they do not wish to hear a continuance of my argument, and therefore wish them wound up before the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue awakes from his slumber and returns to his place. I would suggest to the right hon. leader of the House now that as I most earnestly desire to address myself to the minister from British Columbia when he is here, it being now midnight, it is an opportune time to move that the committee rise, and therefore, with your permission, Mr. Chairman, I would renew my motion that the committee rise and report progress.
Progress reported.
